In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
﴿The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an. He created man. He taught him speech.﴾ Know that the connection (munasabah) of this surah with what precedes it is in two respects. The first: Allah the Exalted opened the previous surah with mention of a miracle that indicates might, majesty and awe, namely the splitting of the moon, for whoever can split the moon can crush the mountains and cut down men. He opened this surah with mention of a miracle that indicates mercy and tenderness, namely the Noble Qur'an, for the healing of hearts comes through purity from sins. The second: He, the Exalted, mentioned in the previous surah ﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ many times, and mentioned in this surah ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13] again and again, because, as we have explained, that surah is a surah manifesting awe and this surah is a surah manifesting mercy. Moreover, the beginning of this surah is connected with the end of what precedes it, where He said at the end of that surah ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]; and "might" (iqtidar) points to awe and greatness. Here He said "al-Rahman," meaning: mighty, severe in punishment, avenger, all-powerful with respect to the disbelievers and the wicked; merciful, bountiful, forgiving to the righteous. Then in the exegesis there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the word "al-Rahman" there are discussions, some of which cannot be clarified except after discussing the word "Allah." So we say:

The first discussion: Some people say that "Allah" with the definite article is a proper name (ism 'alam) for the Originator of possible things. On this basis, some said "al-Rahman" is also a proper name for Him, and they relied on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra: 110], i.e., whichever of the two you call. Some permitted the saying "O al-Rahman" just as "O Allah" is permitted, and relied on the verse. All of this is weak, and some of it is weaker than others. As for their saying that "Allah" with the definite article is a proper name, there is some weakness in it, because if it were so, the hamza in it would be original (asliyyah), and it would not be permissible to make it a connecting hamza (wasliyyah), and it would have to be said "khalaqa Allah" as one says "'alima Ahmad" and "fahima Isma'il." Rather, the truth in it is one of two views: either we say ilah or lah is a proper name for the Originator of possible things, and then it was used with the definite article as in al-Fadl, al-'Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Khalil. On this basis,
Page 74
whoever names another as "ilah" is like one who, for a newborn, uses "Muhammad" and "Ahmad" even if they are proper names used earlier for others; this is permissible, because one who names his son does not have such authority to be obeyed that would prevent others from being named with it, nor does he have the right to monopolize the name for himself or his child. This differs from an obeyed king who has appropriated a name for himself, such that no one under his rule dares, as long as he holds the kingship, to name his son or himself with that name, especially a subject who cannot name himself with the king's name or his son with it. Allah the Exalted is the obeyed King, and everyone else is under His command; so when He has appropriated a name for Himself, it is not permissible for servants to bear that name, and whoever does so has transgressed. Thus the polytheists in naming are transgressors and in meaning are astray. Or we say ilah or lah is a name for whatever is worshipped, and the definite article is for definiteness; and since the meaning is impossible for anyone other than Allah, the name is impossible too. If it is said: then if someone named his son with it, it should be permissible? We say: it is not permissible, because it suggests that it is a name set for that son for a meaning, not for being a proper name. If it is said: naming one with "the Generous" and "the Loving" is permissible? We say: whatever can be understood as a proper name or as a name for a meaning noticed in the mentioned word, without leading to any defect, may be permitted in that case, so naming one with "the Generous" and "the Loving" is permissible; but naming Him "the Creator" or "the Eternal" is not permissible, because if it is taken as a proper name without the meaning being considered, it is permissible, while if it is taken as a name for a meaning that subsists in Him, like the power by which creation subsists or ceases, it is not permissible. But the name of the Worshipped belongs to this category, so naming with it is not permissible. So one of these two views is correct, and their saying "with the definite article it is a proper name" is not correct. Having understood the discussion of "Allah," what follows from it is that "al-Rahman" is a name weaker than that, and permitting "O al-Rahman" is weaker than all of it.

The second discussion: "Allah" and "al-Rahman" with respect to Allah the Exalted are like the first name, and the dominant attribute which becomes like a name after the first name, as in our saying "Umar al-Faruq," "Ali al-Murtada," "Musa al-Rida," and other things we find in the names and attributes of the caliphs, which identify them, which were attributes for them but by frequency of use left the status of attributes, so that even a person who does not have that attribute, or whom the attribute has left, is called by it as a proper name. Thus "al-Rahman" has a specificity to Allah the Exalted, just as those attributes have specificity to those persons; except that in those names and attributes the coining was permissible for the reason we explained, since people are equal in power and greatness, but it is not permissible with respect to Allah the Exalted. If it is said: some people applied the name "al-Rahman" to al-Yamami, we say: that is like how some people applied the name "Ilah" to other than Allah, in transgression and disbelief, considering its permissibility linguistically; and this is a false belief.

The third discussion: Allah the Exalted has two mercies: the preceding and the subsequent. The preceding is that by which He created creation; the subsequent is that by which He gave creation after bringing them into existence, of provision, understanding and other things. So with regard to the preceding mercy He is "al-Rahman," and with regard to the subsequent He is "al-Rahim." That is why it is said: "O Rahman of this world and Rahim of the Hereafter." He is "al-Rahman" because He created creation first by His mercy; since no one else possesses this mercy, and no one creates anyone, it is not permissible to say "al-Rahman" of anyone else. When the righteous among His servants take on some of His characteristics to the extent of human capacity, feeding the hungry and clothing the naked, some of the subsequent mercy by which there is provision and help is found, so it is permissible to call such a person "al-Rahim." We have mentioned all of this in the exegesis of Surat al-Fatihah, but we wanted what we mentioned here to be joined to what we mentioned there, so we have repeated it here, for all of this is like an elaboration of what we mentioned in al-Fatihah.

Page 75
The second issue: "al-Rahman" is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the verbal clause which is His saying "He taught the Qur'an." It was also said that "al-Rahman" is the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being "He is al-Rahman," and then He brought a clause after a clause, saying "He taught the Qur'an." The first is more correct; and on the weak view, "al-Rahman" is a verse on its own.

The third issue: His saying "He taught the Qur'an" must have a second object (maf'ul thani), so what is it? We say the answer to it is from two aspects. The first: it was said that "'allama" here means "made it a sign," i.e., it is a sign of prophethood and a miracle; and this fits His saying "and the moon split" [al-Qamar: 1], as we have explained that He mentioned at the beginning of that surah a miracle of the kind of form, namely that He split what no one else can split; and He mentions in this surah a miracle of the kind of mercy, namely that He spread out of knowledge what no one else can spread, which is what is in the Qur'an. On this aspect of the answer there is another possibility: that He made it such that it is taught, so it is like His saying "And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance" [al-Qamar: 40], and teaching on this aspect is a metaphor. It is said: if one spends on a student and gives him a wage for teaching him, he has taught him. The second: the second object must be there, and it is Jibril and the other angels, whom He taught the Qur'an, and then sent it down upon His servant, as the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193, 194]. It may be said that the second object is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this there is an indication that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Exalted, not the speech of Muhammad. There is a third aspect: that He the Exalted taught the Qur'an to man, and this is closer, so that the blessing may be more complete; and the surah opens to explain the more general of the comprehensive blessings.

The fourth issue: why did He omit the second object? We say: to indicate that the blessing lies in generalizing the teaching, not in teaching one particular person rather than another. It is said: "So-and-so feeds food," to indicate his generosity, without specifying whom he feeds.

The fifth issue: what is the meaning of teaching? We say, on our view that it has a second object, it is conveying knowledge of it. If it is said: how is His saying "He taught the Qur'an" understood alongside His saying "and none knows its interpretation except Allah" [Al 'Imran: 7]? We say: whoever does not stop at His saying "except Allah" and conjoins "those firmly rooted in knowledge" to Allah as a conjunction of a single term to a single term, this objection does not arise for him; and whoever stops and conjoins His saying "and those firmly rooted in knowledge" to His saying "and none knows its interpretation," as a conjunction of one sentence to another sentence, says: He the Exalted knows the Qur'an, because whoever knows a great book and has come to grasp what is in it, and there are difficult passages in it, knows what is in those passages to the extent possible; one says: so-and-so knows and masters that book to the best of his ability, even if he does not know the author's intended meaning with certainty; and the same applies to the teaching of the Qur'an. Or you say: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah," and as for others, they do not know by their own accord what they have not been taught; so this is an indication that the Book of Allah the Exalted is not like other books from which what is in them is extracted by the strength of intelligence and learning.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿He created man. He taught him speech.﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the order, it is in two respects. The first: what we mentioned, that the intended meaning of "'allama" is that He taught the angels, and His teaching the angels was before the creation of man; so He taught His honored angels the Qur'an in truth, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77–79], then the Exalted said: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 80], indicating its sending down after its teaching. On this basis there is an added beauty in the arrangement, in that He mentioned heavenly matters and earthly matters, and paired every heavenly matter with an earthly one, and put heavenly matters before earthly ones until the end of the verses. So He said "He taught the Qur'an," indicating the teaching of the heavenly ones, and said "He taught him speech," indicating the teaching of
Page 76
the earthly ones; and He said "the sun and the moon" [al-Rahman: 5] among heavenly matters, and in opposition to them among earthly ones: "and the star and the tree prostrate" [al-Rahman: 6]. Then He said: ﴿And the heaven—He raised it﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and in opposition to it: ﴿And the earth—He laid it out﴾ [al-Rahman: 10]. The second: the placing of the teaching of the Qur'an first indicates that it is the most complete blessing and the greatest favour; then He explained the manner of teaching the Qur'an, saying: ﴿He created man. He taught him speech.﴾ This is like the saying of one who says: "I taught so-and-so good manners; I carried him upon it, and I spent my wealth on him"; so his saying "I carried him" and "I spent" is an explanation of what preceded; and He placed that first because it is the great favour.

The second issue: what is the difference between this surah and Surat al-'Alaq, where He said there: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], then said: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾ [al-'Alaq: 3, 4], placing creation before teaching? We say: in that surah He did not explicitly mention teaching the Qur'an, so it is like the teaching He mentioned in this surah with His saying "He taught him speech" after His saying "He created man."

Question Three: What is meant by "al-Insan" (the human being)? We say: it is the species (al-jins). It was also said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). And it was said: it refers to Adam. The first view is more sound when considering the wording in "khalaqa" (He created). It includes Muhammad, Adam, and the other prophets.

Question Four: What is al-bayan (eloquent speech/clear expression), and how was it taught? We say: Among the exegetes is one who said: al-bayan is speech (al-mantiq). So He taught him what he speaks with, and that by which others understand what is in him, for through it man is distinguished from the other animals. His saying, ﴿He created man﴾, is an indication of the determination of the creation of his particular body, and ﴿He taught him al-bayan﴾ is an indication of his being distinguished by knowledge from others. What we mentioned first has made clear that al-bayan is the Qur'an, and He repeated it in order to detail what He had mentioned in summary by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, as we said in the example where the speaker says: "I taught so-and-so good manners, I carried him upon them." On this basis, al-bayan is a verbal noun (masdar) by which is meant that which the verbal noun denotes. The use of "al-bayan" in the sense of "the Qur'an," applied to the Qur'an within the Qur'an, is frequent. Exalted is He said: ﴿This is a clear statement (bayan) for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 138]. Allah, exalted is He, has named the Qur'an "furqan" (criterion) and "bayan," and al-bayan is a criterion between truth and falsehood. Thus, the application of "al-bayan" with the intended meaning of the Qur'an is sound.

Question Five: Why did He explicitly mention the two objects in His teaching of al-bayan, but did not explicitly mention them in His teaching of the Qur'an? We say: If we say that what is meant by His saying "He taught the Qur'an" is that He taught man the Qur'an, then we say: He omitted it (the object) because of the greatness of the blessing of teaching, and He placed the mention of it before the one who taught him and before the explanation of his creation. Then He detailed the explanation of how the Qur'an was taught, saying: ﴿He created man﴾, ﴿taught him﴾, and this has explained it. And if we say that what is meant by ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ is the angels, then this is because the purpose is enumerating the blessings upon man, demanding his gratitude, and preventing him from denying it. His teaching of the angels does not appear to man as a benefit returning to man, whereas the teaching of man is a manifest blessing. So He said: ﴿He taught him al-bayan﴾, meaning He taught man, enumerating the blessings upon him. A similar statement is made regarding ﴿Read﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 1]. He said once: ﴿He taught by the pen﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 4] without mentioning who was taught, then He said again: ﴿He taught man what he did not know﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 5], which is al-bayan. It may be argued from this verse that languages are tawqifi (divinely taught), the knowledge of them having been obtained through the teaching of Allah.

We say: whoever does not stop at His saying "except Allah" and conjoins "those firmly rooted in knowledge" to Allah as a conjunction of a single term to a single term, this objection does not arise for him; and whoever stops and conjoins His saying "and those firmly rooted in knowledge" to His saying "and none knows its interpretation," as a conjunction of one sentence to another sentence, says: He the Exalted knows the Qur'an, because whoever knows a great book and has come to grasp what is in it, and there are difficult passages in it, knows what is in those passages to the extent possible; one says: so-and-so knows and masters that book to the best of his ability, even if he does not know the author's intended meaning with certainty; and the same applies to the teaching of the Qur'an. Or you say: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah," and as for others, they do not know by their own accord what they have not been taught; so this is an indication that the Book of Allah the Exalted is not like other books from which what is in them is extracted by the strength of intelligence and learning.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿He created man. He taught him speech.﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: concerning the order, it is in two respects. The first: what we mentioned, that the intended meaning of "'allama" is that He taught the angels, and His teaching the angels was before the creation of man; so He taught His honored angels the Qur'an in truth, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77–79], then the Exalted said: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 80], indicating its sending down after its teaching. On this basis there is an added beauty in the arrangement, in that He mentioned heavenly matters and earthly matters, and paired every heavenly matter with an earthly one, and put heavenly matters before earthly ones until the end of the verses. So He said "He taught the Qur'an," indicating the teaching of the heavenly ones, and said "He taught him speech," indicating the teaching of
Page 76
the earthly ones; and He said "the sun and the moon" [al-Rahman: 5] among heavenly matters, and in opposition to them among earthly ones: "and the star and the tree prostrate" [al-Rahman: 6]. Then He said: ﴿And the heaven—He raised it﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and in opposition to it: ﴿And the earth—He laid it out﴾ [al-Rahman: 10]. The second: the placing of the teaching of the Qur'an first indicates that it is the most complete blessing and the greatest favour; then He explained the manner of teaching the Qur'an, saying: ﴿He created man. He taught him speech.﴾ This is like the saying of one who says: "I taught so-and-so good manners; I carried him upon it, and I spent my wealth on him"; so his saying "I carried him" and "I spent" is an explanation of what preceded; and He placed that first because it is the great favour.

The second issue: what is the difference between this surah and Surat al-'Alaq, where He said there: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], then said: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen﴾ [al-'Alaq: 3, 4], placing creation before teaching? We say: in that surah He did not explicitly mention teaching the Qur'an, so it is like the teaching He mentioned in this surah with His saying "He taught him speech" after His saying "He created man."

Question Three: What is meant by "al-Insan" (the human being)? We say: it is the species (al-jins). It was also said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). And it was said: it refers to Adam. The first view is more sound when considering the wording in "khalaqa" (He created). It includes Muhammad, Adam, and the other prophets.

Question Four: What is al-bayan (eloquent speech/clear expression), and how was it taught? We say: Among the exegetes is one who said: al-bayan is speech (al-mantiq). So He taught him what he speaks with, and that by which others understand what is in him, for through it man is distinguished from the other animals. His saying, ﴿He created man﴾, is an indication of the determination of the creation of his particular body, and ﴿He taught him al-bayan﴾ is an indication of his being distinguished by knowledge from others. What we mentioned first has made clear that al-bayan is the Qur'an, and He repeated it in order to detail what He had mentioned in summary by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, as we said in the example where the speaker says: "I taught so-and-so good manners, I carried him upon them." On this basis, al-bayan is a verbal noun (masdar) by which is meant that which the verbal noun denotes. The use of "al-bayan" in the sense of "the Qur'an," applied to the Qur'an within the Qur'an, is frequent. Exalted is He said: ﴿This is a clear statement (bayan) for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 138]. Allah, exalted is He, has named the Qur'an "furqan" (criterion) and "bayan," and al-bayan is a criterion between truth and falsehood. Thus, the application of "al-bayan" with the intended meaning of the Qur'an is sound.

Question Five: Why did He explicitly mention the two objects in His teaching of al-bayan, but did not explicitly mention them in His teaching of the Qur'an? We say: If we say that what is meant by His saying "He taught the Qur'an" is that He taught man the Qur'an, then we say: He omitted it (the object) because of the greatness of the blessing of teaching, and He placed the mention of it before the one who taught him and before the explanation of his creation. Then He detailed the explanation of how the Qur'an was taught, saying: ﴿He created man﴾, ﴿taught him﴾, and this has explained it. And if we say that what is meant by ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ is the angels, then this is because the purpose is enumerating the blessings upon man, demanding his gratitude, and preventing him from denying it. His teaching of the angels does not appear to man as a benefit returning to man, whereas the teaching of man is a manifest blessing. So He said: ﴿He taught him al-bayan﴾, meaning He taught man, enumerating the blessings upon him. A similar statement is made regarding ﴿Read﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 1]. He said once: ﴿He taught by the pen﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 4] without mentioning who was taught, then He said again: ﴿He taught man what he did not know﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 5], which is al-bayan. It may be argued from this verse that languages are tawqifi (divinely taught), the knowledge of them having been obtained through the teaching of Allah.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾ ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate themselves﴾. Regarding the order, there are several aspects:

The first: When God's being the Most Merciful (al-Rahman) was established, and He pointed to that which is healing and mercy, namely the Qur'an, He mentioned His blessings and began with the creation of man, for man is a blessing, and all blessings are completed by him; were he not existent, nothing would be benefited from. Then He explained the blessing of perception with His words: ﴿He taught him eloquent speech﴾, and this is like existence, for without it there would be no benefit nor benefiting. Then He mentioned from among the observable things two apparent blessings, which are the most manifest kinds of heavenly blessings, namely the sun and the moon. Were it not for the sun, darkness would not have dispersed; were it not for the moon, many of the apparent blessings would be lost. This is unlike the other stars, for their blessings do not appear to everyone as the blessing of these two appears. Then He explained the perfection of their benefit in their movement by a reckoning that does not change. Were the sun fixed in one place, no one would benefit from it; and were its course not known to creatures, they would not benefit from cultivation at its proper times, nor would affairs be built upon the seasons. Then, in contrast to these two, He explained two apparent blessings from the earth, namely the plant that has no stem and the plant that has a stem, for provision originates from it. Were it not for plants, there would be no provision for the child of Adam except what God wills. The root of blessings lies in abundant provision. We only said that the plant is the origin of provision because provision is either vegetal or animal, such as meat, milk and other parts of animals; were it not for plants, animals would not live, and plants are the origin. Plants are of two kinds: that which stands upon a stem, such as wheat, barley, large trees and the roots of fruits; and that which does not stand upon a stem, such as herbs spread upon the earth, grasses and the herbage that is the food of animals.

The second: When God mentioned the Qur'an, and it was sufficient, needing no other proof along with it, He said after it: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾ ﴿and the star and the tree﴾, and other signs, as an indication that for some people, if they have the pure soul that God enriches with the proofs found in the Qur'an, then for them there are signs on the horizons, among them the sun and the moon. He chose these two for mention because their motion according to a reckoning indicates a chooser agent who subjected them in a specific manner. Even if all in the world, the naturalists, the philosophers and others, gathered and agreed to fix their motion on the specific course, with the correct specific manner and the known measure of slowness and speed, none of them would reach his aim to the point of returning to the truth and saying: God moved them as He willed. He mentioned the earth, the heaven and others as an indication of the rational proofs we have mentioned, which confirm the transmitted proofs found in the Qur'an.

The third: We have mentioned that this surah opens with a miracle indicating it, from the aspect of its form. So He mentioned the miracle of the Qur'an in a way that is a reply to those who deny prophethood, in the manner we have pointed out. That is: God sent down the Book to His Prophet and sent him to mankind with the noblest address. Some deniers said: How is it possible for a body to descend from the heaven to the earth, and how can what is on the earth ascend to the heaven? God said: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾, indicating that their motion is by a chooser mover, not a natural one, and they agreed with us on this. They said: rotational motion cannot be natural and voluntary. So we say: He who moved the sun and the moon in a circular manner, sent down the angels in a straight line; then the star and the tree move upward in a straight line, although the heavy, according to your doctrine, does not ascend upward. That is by God's power and will. Likewise, the motion of the angel is possible, like the orbit. As for His words ﴿by a reckoning﴾, in it is an indication of the answer to their saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8]. That is because He, exalted is He, as He chose for their motion a specific course, a known direction and a particular measure, likewise He chose for the angel a known time and a specific course by His grace.

In the interpretation there are discussions:

The first: What is the wisdom in His describing what returns to God, exalted is He, when He said of them: ﴿by a reckoning﴾, and did not say: God moved them by a reckoning, or subjected them, or caused them to run, as He said: ﴿He created man﴾ and said: ﴿He taught him eloquent speech﴾? We say: there are wisdoms in it, among them that it is an indication that the creation of man and his being taught eloquent speech is more complete and greater than the creation of benefits for him such as provision and other things, since there He explicitly stated that He is its doer and maker, and here He did not state it explicitly. Among them: that His words ﴿the sun and the moon﴾ here, with such magnitude, is like someone who says: I have given you thousands and hundreds many times, and you have received units and tens many times, and you did not thank me; its meaning is: you have received from me and from my giving, but he specifies explicit mention of the giving for the abundant. Among them: since we explained that His words ﴿the sun and the moon﴾ are an indication of a rational proof confirming the transmitted one, and He did not say explicitly "I did," as an indication that it is intelligible; if you look at it, you will know that it is from Me and you will acknowledge it. As for the transmitted proof, He explicitly stated what returns to it of the act.

The second: In what manner is the particle "bi" in ﴿bi-husban﴾ connected? We say: it is clear from its interpretation, and the interpretation has also been explained and has come out from another aspect. So we say: in ḥusbān there are two aspects. The first, the well-known one: that the intended meaning is calculation; one says: he calculated a calculation and a reckoning. On this view the "bi" is for accompaniment; you say: you came with good, that is, together with good and accompanied by good. Likewise the sun and the moon run, and with them is their reckoning. Similar to it: ﴿Indeed We created everything by measure﴾ and ﴿and everything with Him is by measure﴾. It may also be for assistance, as in your saying: "By the help of God I prevailed," and "By the success of God I performed the pilgrimage." Likewise they run by a reckoning from God. The second aspect: ḥusbān is the orbit, likening it to the ḥusbān of the millstone, which is that which turns and so turns the stone. On this view it is for instrumentality, as is said of instruments: "I wrote with the pen." So they revolve by the orbit, and this is like His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Saba: 40]. The third: on the well-known aspect, is each one running by its own reckoning, or both by one reckoning? What is intended? We say: both are possible. If we look at each of them, then each has a separate reckoning, as in His saying: ﴿each in an orbit﴾, not meaning that all are gathered in one orbit, and as in His saying: ﴿and everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. If we look to God, exalted is He, then all have one reckoning, the measure of the whole by determining their reckoning by a reckoning. An example: one who divides his estate among his heirs, giving each a known share by one reckoning; then the matter differs among them, so one takes a sixth, another takes so much, another so much; likewise the one reckoning.

As for His words ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate themselves﴾, there are also discussions in it:

The first: What is the wisdom in mentioning the preceding sentences without a coordinating particle, and here He mentioned it with a coordinating "wa"? We say: so that the speech may vary into two kinds. For one who counts blessings upon another sometimes mentions them in a sequence without a particle, saying: So-and-so has bestowed much upon you; he enriched you after poverty, honored you after humiliation, strengthened you after weakness. And at other times he mentions them with a coordinating particle, which may be "wa," or "fa," or "thumma," saying: So-and-so honored you, bestowed upon you, and did you good; he raised you, taught you, and enriched you; he gave you, then enriched you, then made people need you. Likewise here He mentioned the enumeration with both kinds. If it is said: explain more and clarify the difference between the two kinds in meaning, we say: the one who speaks without a particle seems to intend the explanation of many blessings, so he leaves out the particle to encompass all without lengthening speech. For this reason that kind is mostly used when blessings exceed three, or when they are more than two. If he mentions it with two blessings, he says: So-and-so gave you wealth and married you to a daughter; this indicates many blessings, and he limited himself to two only as an example. The one who speaks with a particle seems to intend to draw attention to the independence of each blessing by itself, and to remove the illusion of substitution and explanation, for the speaker's saying "he bestowed blessing upon you, he gave you wealth" is an explanation of the first; so there is no mention of two blessings together in his speech, unlike when it is mentioned with a particle. If it is said: if this is as you described, would it be closer to eloquence if He had mentioned the first blessings with "wa," then at the lengthening of speech at the end had listed them in a row? The revelation of His speech in this manner suffices as evidence that what God mentioned is more eloquent, and there is a detailed apparent proof explained by investigation: speech may begin with the speaker intending brevity, but circumstances require lengthening, either because a questioner asks much, or a seeker desires increase because of the grace of the speaker's words, or for other reasons. And it may begin intending elaboration and detail, but then something arises requiring restriction to the intended purpose, due to the burden on the listener or the speaker, and other things found in human speech. We say: God's speech has its benefits for His servants, not for Himself. So in this surah He began the matter by indicating the explanation of the most complete blessings, since that is the aim; so He brought what is specific to abundance. Then, the human being is not of perfect knowledge, knowing the speaker's intent when the speech is from his fellow kind; how much more so when the speech is the speech of God, exalted is He. So God began with it for the other benefit: to remove the illusion of substitution and explanation, and to emphasize that each of them is a complete blessing. If it is said: if that is so, what is the wisdom in specifying the coordination with this statement and beginning with it, rather than with what precedes it or follows it? We say: so that the two kinds may be equal. He mentioned eight blessings, such as teaching the Qur'an, creating man, and others: four of them without "wa," and four with "wa." As for His words ﴿therein is fruit and the palm﴾ [al-Rahman: 11] and His words ﴿and the grain with its husk﴾ [al-Rahman: 12], they are for explaining the blessing of the earth in detail. Then in choosing eight there is a subtle point: seven is a complete number, and eight is seven with an addition, so there is an indication that God's blessings exceed the limit of enumeration, since what exceeds completeness is not specific and defined. So He mentioned eight of them as an indication of the excess beyond the limit of the number, not to indicate confinement to it.

* * *

The second issue: What is "the star" (al-najm)? We say: there are two views:
One: the plant that has no stem.
The second: the star of the sky. The first is more apparent, because He mentioned it with the tree in contrast to the sun and the moon, mentioning two earths in contrast to two heavens. Also, His words ﴿prostrate themselves﴾ indicate that the intended meaning is not the star of the sky, for whoever interpreted it that way said: it prostrates at its setting; and in that case the sun and the moon also set, so there would be no benefit in the specification. But if we say they are two earths, we say: ﴿prostrate themselves﴾ in the sense that their shadows prostrate, so prostration is specific to them and not to the sun and the moon. As for their prostration, there are several aspects:
The first: what we have mentioned, the prostration of shadows.
The second: their submission to God, exalted is He, and their emergence from the earth, their continuance and their standing upon it by God's permission. He subjected the sun and the moon to a circular motion, and the star to an upward straight motion; so He likened the plant standing in its place to prostration, because the one who prostrates remains still.

Third: The reality of prostration exists in both of them, even if it is not visible, just as each of them glorifies (God) even if it is not understood, as the Exalted said: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra: 44].

Fourth: Prostration is placing the forehead or the front of the head on the ground. The star and the tree, in reality, have their heads on the ground and their feet in the air, because the head of an animal is that by which it drinks and nourishes itself, and the star and the tree nourish and drink through their roots. Also, life cannot remain without the head, whereas neither the tree nor the star remains intact and fresh when the roots are damaged, but it remains when its branches and tops are cut off. It is only said that the branches have "heads of trees" because the head in a human is that which is toward the upper direction, so the tops of trees were called "heads." Having understood this, the star and the tree always have their heads on the ground, so their prostration is by resemblance, not in the strict sense.

The third issue: The mention of the star before the tree is a verbal correspondence with the sun and the moon, and there is also a meaningful reason: the star is more suited to the meaning of prostration because it spreads over the earth like one who truly prostrates, just as the sun is more suited to reckoning (al-husban), because calculating its course is easier for the astronomers (al-muqawwimin) than calculating the course of the moon, since nothing is more difficult for the astronomers than determining the moon's position in the calculation of the zij (astronomical tables).

So God began with it for the other benefit: to remove the illusion of substitution and explanation, and to emphasize that each of them is a complete blessing. If it is said: if that is so, what is the wisdom in specifying the coordination with this statement and beginning with it, rather than with what precedes it or follows it? We say: so that the two kinds may be equal. He mentioned eight blessings, such as teaching the Qur'an, creating man, and others: four of them without "wa," and four with "wa." As for His words ﴿therein is fruit and the palm﴾ [al-Rahman: 11] and His words ﴿and the grain with its husk﴾ [al-Rahman: 12], they are for explaining the blessing of the earth in detail. Then in choosing eight there is a subtle point: seven is a complete number, and eight is seven with an addition, so there is an indication that God's blessings exceed the limit of enumeration, since what exceeds completeness is not specific and defined. So He mentioned eight of them as an indication of the excess beyond the limit of the number, not to indicate confinement to it.

* * *

The second issue: What is "the star" (al-najm)? We say: there are two views:
One: the plant that has no stem.
The second: the star of the sky. The first is more apparent, because He mentioned it with the tree in contrast to the sun and the moon, mentioning two earths in contrast to two heavens. Also, His words ﴿prostrate themselves﴾ indicate that the intended meaning is not the star of the sky, for whoever interpreted it that way said: it prostrates at its setting; and in that case the sun and the moon also set, so there would be no benefit in the specification. But if we say they are two earths, we say: ﴿prostrate themselves﴾ in the sense that their shadows prostrate, so prostration is specific to them and not to the sun and the moon. As for their prostration, there are several aspects:
The first: what we have mentioned, the prostration of shadows.
The second: their submission to God, exalted is He, and their emergence from the earth, their continuance and their standing upon it by God's permission. He subjected the sun and the moon to a circular motion, and the star to an upward straight motion; so He likened the plant standing in its place to prostration, because the one who prostrates remains still.

Third: The reality of prostration exists in both of them, even if it is not visible, just as each of them glorifies (God) even if it is not understood, as the Exalted said: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra: 44].

Fourth: Prostration is placing the forehead or the front of the head on the ground. The star and the tree, in reality, have their heads on the ground and their feet in the air, because the head of an animal is that by which it drinks and nourishes itself, and the star and the tree nourish and drink through their roots. Also, life cannot remain without the head, whereas neither the tree nor the star remains intact and fresh when the roots are damaged, but it remains when its branches and tops are cut off. It is only said that the branches have "heads of trees" because the head in a human is that which is toward the upper direction, so the tops of trees were called "heads." Having understood this, the star and the tree always have their heads on the ground, so their prostration is by resemblance, not in the strict sense.

The third issue: The mention of the star before the tree is a verbal correspondence with the sun and the moon, and there is also a meaningful reason: the star is more suited to the meaning of prostration because it spreads over the earth like one who truly prostrates, just as the sun is more suited to reckoning (al-husban), because calculating its course is easier for the astronomers (al-muqawwimin) than calculating the course of the moon, since nothing is more difficult for the astronomers than determining the moon's position in the calculation of the zij (astronomical tables).

Then Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And the sky—He raised it high and set up the balance﴾

The raising of the sky is known in meaning, and its being in the accusative is known in form: it is governed by a verb which is explained by His words "﴿raised it﴾," as if He, exalted is He, had said: "He raised the sky." It has also been recited as "wa-as-samā'u" (with the nominative) on the basis of the inceptive (ibtida') and as a conjunction (ʿatf) to the nominal sentence which is His words "﴿the sun and the moon﴾." As for "﴿and set up the balance﴾," it is an indication of justice (ʿadl). In it there is a subtle point: Exalted is He began first with knowledge, then mentioned that in which is the noblest of the kinds of knowledge, which is the Qur'an, then mentioned justice and mentioned the most specific of the matters related to it, which is the balance (mīzān). This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾" [al-Hadid: 25], so that people act by the Book and do with the balance what the Book commands them. So His saying "﴿Taught the Qur'an﴾" and "﴿set up the balance﴾" is like "﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾."

If it is said: knowledge is undoubtedly a great blessing, but as for the balance, what great blessing is in it by which it is counted among the favours? We say: souls dislike being cheated, and no one is content for another to overcome him even in a small matter, and he regards that as contempt toward him, so he does not leave it to his opponent out of a desire to prevail. No one thinks that his opponent overcomes him; so, were it not for clarification followed by equality, Satan would have cast enmity among people, as happens in ignorance, loss of reason and intoxication. Just as reason and knowledge became the means for the continuation of the prosperity of the world, so justice in wisdom is a means, and the most specific of these means is the balance. Thus it is a complete blessing, and one should not look at the fact that its blessing is not apparent because of its abundance and the ease of access to it, like air and water, whose excellence is not clear except when they are lost.

Then God said, Exalted is He: ﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾ ﴿and establish the weight with justice﴾. On this basis it has been said: the intended meaning of the first "balance" is justice (*'adl*), and "placing" it means "legislating" it. It is as if He said: God legislated justice so that you would not transgress in the balance, which is the instrument of justice. This is what has been transmitted. However, the better view is that the matter be reversed, so that it is said: the first "balance" is the instrument, and the second is in the sense of the verbal noun (*masdar*), and its meaning is: He placed the balance so that you would not transgress in the weighing, or in the sense of justice, which is giving every entitled party its right. It is as if He said: He placed the instrument so that you would not transgress in giving those who are entitled their rights. It is also permissible to intend the verbal noun by "balance," as the intention of *wuthuq* (trust) by *mithaq* (covenant) and of *wa'd* (promise) by *mi'ad* (appointment). Thus the intended meaning of "balance" is the instrument of weighing.

The second aspect: "an" (that) is explanatory (*mufassirah*), and the estimated meaning is: He legislated justice, that is, "do not transgress." So "placing the balance" means "legislating justice." Applying "placing" to legislation and "balance" to justice is permissible. It may also be said: "He placed the balance," meaning the weighing.

As for His saying ﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾, on this aspect the intended meaning is the weighing. It is as if He forbade transgression in weighing and in being balanced (*ittizan*). The repetition of "balance" with the same wording indicates that both refer to one thing. It is as if He said: "That you not transgress in it." If it is asked: if the intended meaning were weighing, would He not have said "that you not transgress in the weighing"? We answer: if He had said "in the weighing," one would assume that the prohibition concerns weighing for others only, not being balanced oneself. So it was expressed with the word for the instrument, which encompasses both taking and giving. This is because the giver, if he weighs and tips the scale noticeably, has indeed gained excess, especially in currency exchange and in selling like for like.

His saying ﴿and establish the weight with justice﴾ indicates that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ is "that you not transgress in the weighing," because His saying ﴿and establish the weight﴾ serves as an explanation of His saying ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾, namely, departing from establishing it with justice. [Page 81] His saying ﴿and establish the weight with justice﴾ admits of two aspects. The first: "establish" (*aqimu*) means "stand by it," as in His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-An'am: 72], that is, "stand by it constantly." This is because the verb is sometimes transitive through a preposition and sometimes through the added hamza; you say "adhhabahu" (he took it away) and "dhahaba bihi" (he went away with it). The second: "establish" means "stand," as one says: "in the wood I set it up and straightened it" (*aqamtuhu wa-qawwamtuhu*). And *al-qist* means justice. If it is asked: how did *qasata* come to mean "to act unjustly" and not "to be just"? We answer: *al-qist* is a noun, not a verbal noun. Nouns that are not verbal nouns, when someone brings them or finds them, are said of with the form *af'ala* in the sense of "to make it exist." Thus one says: "Fulan *atrafa*, *atḥafa*, and *a'rafa*," meaning he brought a rarity, a gift, or recognition. One says: "*aqbaḍa al-sayf*" (he gave the sword a hilt), "*a'lama al-thawb*" (he put a mark on the garment), "*a'lama*" (he set a sign), and likewise "*alajama al-faras*" (he bridled the horse) and "*asraja*" (he saddled it). So when he commands justice or establishes it, he has done *aqsata*, which means *'adala* (to be just). As for *qasata*, it is *fa'ala* derived from a noun that is not a verbal noun. When a noun is not originally a verbal noun, and a verb is derived from it, it may change it from its original state. An example is "*kataf*" (shoulder): when you say "*kattaftuhu kitafan*," it is as if you said: "I removed it from what it was in terms of usefulness and changed it." The meaning of "*kattaftuhu*" is "I bound its two shoulders together, so it is bound." So *kataf* and *qist* have both become verbal nouns from a noun, and the verb's meaning has changed from the condition it should be in. On this basis, there is no need to say that *al-qasit* and *al-muqsit* do not share the same origin. In any case, it was possible to say *aqsata* in the sense of "removing *qist*," as one says *ashka* (to remove complaint) or *a'jama* (to remove foreignness). This investigation has a benefit. The speaker's saying "Fulan is more just (*aqsat*) than Fulan," and God's saying ﴿That is more just (*aqsat*) in the sight of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. The basis of the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) is that it be derived from the bare triliteral root, as you say "*azlam*" and "*a'dal*" from *zalim* and *'adil*. Thus *aqsat* should have been derived from *qasit*, but it was not so, because, as we explained, the origin is *qist*, and *qasata* is a verb that is not in the proper manner, while *iqsat* is its removal and the return of *qist* to its origin. So *aqsat* came to agree with the origin. The comparative form is taken from what is the root, not from what is derived from it. Thus one says "*azlam min zalim*" (more unjust than an unjust person), not "*min mutazallim*," and "*a'lam min 'alim*" (more knowledgeable than a knowledgeable person), not "*min mu'allim*." The conclusion is that *al-aqsat*, although it looks to the form, should have been from *al-qasit*. But considering the meaning, it must be from *al-muqsit*, because *al-muqsit* is closer to the root from which it is derived, *al-qist*. This is not the case with *al-zalim* and *al-muzlim*, for *al-azlam* came to be derived from *al-zalim*, because it is closer to the root both in form and meaning. The same holds for *al-'alim* and *al-mu'allim*, and for *al-khabar* and *al-mukhbir*.

Then He said: ﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾, i.e., do not diminish the weighed thing (al-mawzun). God mentioned al-Mizan (the balance/scale) three times, each time with a different meaning. The first is the instrument: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. The second is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar): ﴿do not transgress in the balance﴾, i.e., in the weighing (al-wazn). The third is in the sense of the object weighed: ﴿and do not make the balance deficient﴾, i.e., the weighed thing (al-mawzun). He mentioned all of them with the word al-mizan because, as we have explained, al-mizan is more comprehensive in benefit. It is like the Qur'an (al-Qur'an), which God mentioned in the sense of the verbal noun in His saying: ﴿So follow its Qur'an﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18]; in the sense of the thing recited in His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17]; and in the sense of the book containing the recited text in His saying: ﴿And if only a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. So it is like an instrument and a place for it. And in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 87], and in many places He mentions the Qur'an as the name of this noble Book. There is a correspondence between the Qur'an and the balance, for the Qur'an contains knowledge that is not found in other books, and the balance contains justice that is not found in other instruments.

Page 82

If it is said: What is the benefit in placing the sky before the verb, where He said: ﴿And the sky—He raised it﴾, and placing the verb before the balance, where He said: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾? We say: We have mentioned many times that in every word of God's words there are benefits which the knowledge of mankind does not encompass, except what becomes apparent. The apparent point here is that when He enumerated the eight blessings as we have explained, some of them were more specifically related to humans than others. For that which was most specifically related to humans, He placed the verb first, just as we have explained that a person says: "I gave you thousands and obtained for you tens," so he does not explicitly attribute the action to himself in the case of a small amount. Likewise he says regarding specific blessings: "I gave you such-and-such," but in what is shared, he says: "There reached you from what we divided among ourselves such-and-such." So he explicitly mentions giving when it is specific, and does not attribute the verb to himself when it is shared. Similarly here, He mentioned four matters with the verb placed first: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, ﴿He created man﴾, ﴿He taught him eloquent speech (al-bayan)﴾, ﴿And He set up the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 1–7]; and four matters with the noun placed first: ﴿The sun and the moon [move by precise calculation]﴾, ﴿and the stars and the trees prostrate﴾, ﴿And the sky—He raised it﴾, ﴿And the earth—He spread it﴾, because the benefit of teaching the Qur'an returns more to humans, the creation of man is specifically for them, and teaching them al-bayan and setting up the balance are likewise, since they are the ones who benefit from it—not the angels, nor other than humans among the animals. As for the sun, the moon, the stars, the trees, the sky and the earth, every living creature on the face of the earth and beneath the sky benefits from them.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And the earth He laid out for all living beings.﴾ On this there are several discussions.

The first: It has already been noted that placing the noun before the verb occurs in contexts where exclusivity is not intended. The words of the Exalted, ﴿for all living beings﴾, indicate exclusivity, since the lam (li) denotes the return of benefit. We say: the answer to this is from two aspects. The first is what has been said: that al-anam (living beings) includes humans and other animals, so the words ﴿for all living beings﴾ do not necessitate exclusivity to humans. The second: the earth is laid out for everything upon it, and He specifically mentioned humans because their benefit from it is greatest, for they benefit from it, from what is in it, and from what is upon it. So He said ﴿for all living beings﴾ because of the great benefit that living beings derive from it, if we say that al-anam is humankind. If we say that it refers to creation in general, then "creation" (al-khalq) is often mentioned while meaning humankind in many contexts.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿In it are fruits, and palm trees with sheaths﴾ refer to trees. His words: ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾ [al-Rahman: 12] refer to plants that are not trees. Al-fakiha (fruit) is that which delights the soul, and it is an active participle either in the manner of ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 7], meaning possessing a pleasure in which everyone takes delight, or in the usage of naming an instrument by the form of the agent: one says rawiya (a water-skin) for the waterskin by which the thirsty person is refreshed, and it carries a sense of intensity, like al-rahila (the mount) for that which is ridden upon. Then it became a name for some fruits, initially established without derivation. The indefiniteness (in fakiha) is for multiplicity, meaning abundant, just as one says of so-and-so that he has wealth, meaning great wealth. We have already mentioned the aspect by which indefiniteness indicates greatness: the speaker is, as it were, indicating that it is great, beyond the comprehension of anyone, so its indefiniteness points to its being beyond the possibility of knowing its true nature.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿and the palm trees with sheaths﴾ refer to the other kind of trees, because fruit-bearing trees are the best of trees, and they are divided into trees whose fruits are fruits (not eaten as staple food) and trees whose fruits are a staple and which are also enjoyed as fruit, just as fruit may also be eaten as food, for the hungry person, if he finds nothing but fruits, sustains himself with them, eating them without taking pleasure in them. And here there are discussions:

Page 83
The first: What is the wisdom in placing fruit before staple food? We say: this is the principle of beginning with the lower and ascending to the higher. Fruit is less beneficial than the palm tree from which staple food comes, and the enjoyment of fruit is less than that of grain, on which the main sustenance depends in all contexts, and with which humankind is nourished in all lands. So He began with fruit, then mentioned the palm, then mentioned grain, which is the most complete blessing because it suits human temperament; for this reason God created it in all lands, and He specified the palm for hot lands.

The second discussion: What is the wisdom in indefinite fakiha and definite al-nakhl? Its answer is from several aspects:

The first: staple food is needed at all times, constantly circulating at every moment and season, so it is more known, whereas fruit occurs in some seasons and with some individuals.

The second: fruit, as we have explained, is that with which one enjoys and which delights the soul, and that differs for each person according to each time; whoever is overcome by heat and thirst wants to enjoy sour fruits and the like, while some people want to enjoy sweet ones and the like. So fruit is not specific, and therefore He made it indefinite, while the palm and grain are familiar and known, so He made them definite.

The third: the palm alone is a great blessing, with many benefits attached to it, whereas fruit is a type of it, like peaches and plums, for example, which do not carry the great blessing found in the palm. So He said fakiha (fruit) in the indefinite to indicate abundance, and He explicitly stated abundance in other places, saying: ﴿calling therein for abundant fruit﴾ [Sad: 51], and He said: ﴿and abundant fruit﴾ ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 32–33]. So fruit, which God mentioned and described explicitly as abundant, was mentioned indefinitely so that it is understood as characterized by the abundance appropriate to a blessing within each single kind, unlike the palm.

The third discussion: What is the wisdom in mentioning fruit by its own name rather than by the names of its trees, and mentioning the palm by its own name rather than by the name of its fruit? We say: this was already explained in the surah Ya-Sin, where He said: ﴿from palm trees and vines﴾ [Ya-Sin: 34]. The vine tree, which is the karm, is humble in relation to its fruit, which is the grape, whereas the palm tree is great in relation to its fruit. It contains many benefits, as is known, from making containers from it, benefiting from its heart (al-jummar), from the spathe (al-tal'), the unripe dates (al-busr), the ripe dates (al-rutab), and other things. Its fruit appears at different times, as though they were different fruits. So it is a more complete blessing compared to other trees. He therefore mentioned the palm by its name and mentioned the fruit without its trees, since the benefits of the trees lie within their fruits themselves.

The fourth discussion: What is the meaning of ﴿with sheaths﴾ (dhat al-akmam)? We say: there are two interpretations:

The first: al-akmam is everything that covers, the plural of kumm (with a dammah on the kaf), and it includes its bark, its fibre, and its stones, all of which are useful, just as the palm is useful for its branches and its heart, which is the jummar.

The second: al-akmam is the plural of kimm (with a kasrah on the kaf), which is the sheath of the spathe, for it first appears within a sheath which then splits, and the spathe comes out of it.

If it is said, on the first interpretation: what is the benefit of mentioning ﴿with sheaths﴾? It indicates the kinds of blessings. And on the second interpretation, what is the benefit of mentioning it? We say: it indicates the ease of gathering and benefiting from them, for the palm is a great tree, and its fruit cannot be made to fall by shaking it, so the tree must be climbed. If it were like the sycamore fig (al-jummayz), which is said to bear its fruit scattered one by one, its harvesting would be difficult. So He said ﴿with sheaths﴾, meaning that in each sheath there is much, so that taking a single cluster from it suffices one or two men, like grape clusters. Consider that, for if the grape's berries were scattered on the trees like the sycamore or the hawthorn, it would be impossible to gather them by shaking whenever gathering is desired. God therefore created them in gathered clusters; likewise the ripe dates. Thus their being ﴿with sheaths﴾ is part of completing the favour.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 12–13:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the grain, with its husk, and the sweet-scented plants﴾. He limited the trees to the palm, because it is the greatest of them, and included in "the grain" wheat, barley, and every grain used for food, whether as bread or as a relish. We have explained that He mentioned it later in the enumeration in the manner of ascent (al-irtiqa') step by step, so grains are more beneficial than palms and more widespread in places.

As for His saying, ﴿with its husk﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: the chaff, which benefits our animals that were created for us.

The second: the leaves of the plant that has a stalk, emerging from the sides of the stalk, like the leaves of the ear of grain from its top to its bottom.

The third: "the husk" is the leaf of what is eaten only, and ﴿the sweet-scented plants﴾ has several interpretations. It is said: what is smelled. It is said: the leaves. It is said: it is the well-known basil among us, and its seed is beneficial in medicines. The more evident view is that its head is like a flower, and this is the origin of the existence of the intended purpose, for that flower forms from that grain, and it sets until it ripens. So "the husk" refers to that leaf, and "the sweet-scented plants" refers to that flower. He mentioned both because each of them leads to a purpose: one is fodder for animals, and the other is medicine for humans.

It has been read "al-rayhan" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-'asf" (﴿al-rayhani﴾), and in the nominative, coordinated with "al-habb" (﴿al-rayhanu﴾). This admits two interpretations:

One: that what is meant by "al-rayhan" is what is smelled, so it is a matter distinct from the grain and is therefore coordinated with it.

The second: that the sense is "possessor of the sweet-scented plants," by omitting the first term (al-mudaf) and putting the second term (al-mudaf ilayhi) in its place, as in ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This fits the meaning we mentioned, so that the sweet-scented plant with which He concluded the kinds of earthly blessings is more precious and noble. If what was meant by "al-rayhan" were the well-known plant or the fragrant things, that ordering would not have resulted. It has also been read "wa-al-rayhani" (in the genitive), and only someone who reads ﴿and the grain, with its husk﴾ in that way would read it so, and the two interpretations recur in it.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ On this there are several discussions:

The first: To whom is the address? We say: there are several views:

The first: humans and jinn, and on this there are three opinions:

One: it is said that "al-anam" (creation) is a name for jinn and humans, and it has already been mentioned, so the pronoun returns to what is included in "al-anam" of the kind.

Second: "al-anam" is the name of humans, and ﴿al-jann﴾ (the jinn), since it was intended and became apparent afterward by His saying ﴿and He created the jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 15], it is permissible for the pronoun to return to it. How not, when it is permissible for a pronoun to return to what is intended even though nothing of it has been mentioned? You say: "I do not know which of them is better, Zayd or 'Amr."

Third: that the addressee is in intention, not in the wording, as if He said: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ O you two weighty ones (al-thaqalan).

The second: the male and the female. So the pronoun returns to both of them and the address is with both of them.

The third: "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny? So which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny?" in one wording, and the intention is repetition for emphasis.

The fourth: the intended meaning is generality, but the general term includes two divisions by which the whole is confined, and nothing of the general remains outside it. For when you say: "He created whoever understands and whoever does not understand," or you say: "God knows what appears and what does not appear," and other such exhaustive divisions, generality is implied. So it is as if He said: "O you two kinds: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾" And know that an exhaustive division does not go beyond two matters at its root, and confinement is achieved only by them. If there are more, then there are two kinds one of which has been folded into the other. An example: if you say, "Color is either black or white, or red or yellow, or other," it is as if you said, "Color is either black or not black, or white or not white." Then what is not white is either red or not red, and so on through all the divisions. So He pointed to the two confining kinds, so that no one and nothing may deny the blessings of God.

The fifth: denial may be by the heart without the tongue, as with the hypocrites; it may be by the tongue without the heart, as with the obstinate; and it may be by both together. Denial does not go beyond being by the tongue or by the heart. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "O heart and tongue, so which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" For the blessings have reached a point at which the obstinate cannot persist in denying them.

The sixth: the denier denies the Messenger and the auditory proofs that are in the Qur'an, and denies the reason, the demonstrations, and those in the horizons and in the selves. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "O you two deniers, which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" The signs of prophethood have appeared, for ﴿the Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾; and the signs of unity have appeared, for He created man and taught him expression, raised the sky, and laid down the earth.

The seventh: the denier may be one who denies in fact, or the denial may be from him not yet occurred but anticipated. So God, exalted is He, said: "O denier, you deny and you are engaged in falsehood, and it troubles your breast that you are denying: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾"

These views are close to one another. The most evident of them is the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan), because they are mentioned in the verses of this surah: by His saying ﴿We will attend to you, O you two weighty ones﴾ [al-Rahman: 31], by His saying ﴿O assembly of jinn and humans﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], by His saying ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ and ﴿and He created the jinn﴾, and otherwise. ("The two kinds" [al-zawjan]) is because it occurs much in the Qur'an, and generality by intending two exhaustive kinds covers all. It may be said that generality is better, because if what was meant were the humans and jinn whom He addressed with His saying ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾, He would not say after the creation of man, but would address them and say: "We created you, O man, ﴿from clay﴾, and We created you, O jinn," or He would say, "He created you, O man," because speech became an address with both of them. And when He said "man," this shows that the addressee is other than him, namely the general, so it becomes as if He said: "O creatures and listeners, We created man from clay like pottery, and We created the jinn from a smokeless fire." The rest of the explanation will come in its places in the interpretation of this surah, if God, exalted is He, wills.

The second: What is the wisdom in the address when no addressee has been mentioned? We say: it is of the type of iltifat (shift of grammatical address, al-iltifat), since the structure of the opening of the surah is based on address to everyone who hears. So it is as if, when He said ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾, He said: "Listen, O listeners." The address is for reproach and admonition, as if God, exalted is He, alerted the heedless denier that he should imagine himself standing before his Lord, and his Lord says to him: "I have bestowed upon you such and such," and then says: "So which of My bounties will you deny?" Without doubt, at this point he will feel such shame that the imposition of the third person will not be appropriate to him.

The third: What is the benefit of choosing the word "Lord" (rabb)? If he addresses, he intends the address of one person; so why did He say ﴿your Lord, you two deny﴾, when the one present and speaking is the addressee, so how does He make the denial attributed to the addressee fall upon the absent? Would it not be more appropriate in address to say, "which of My bounties will you two deny?" We say: in the previous surah He said ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 23], ﴿the people of Lut denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 33], and He said ﴿they denied Our signs﴾ [al-Qamar: 42], and He said ﴿so We seized them﴾, and He said ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ [al-Qamar: 16]. All of these are attributed to the pronoun of the speaker, since that was for intimidation. God is too great to be feared, so if He had said "the Powerful seized them" or "the Destroyer," it would not have been as much of an exaltation as His saying ﴿so We seized them﴾ [al-An'am: 42]. For this reason God, exalted is He, said ﴿and God warns you of Himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. This is like the one renowned for strength who says, "I am the one you know," so that in affirming the threat he is above his saying "I am the punisher." Since attribution to the self (al-nafs) was used in that surah at the time of destruction and punishment, in this surah at the explanation of mercy He mentioned a term that removes awe, which is the word "Lord." So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾, and He is your Lord who nurtures you.

The fourth: What is the wisdom in the repetition of this verse and its occurring thirty-one times? We say: the answer to it is from several aspects:

The first: the benefit of repetition is affirmation. As for this particular number, numbers are tawqifiyya (fixed by revelation, not something minds can reach by estimating their measures). It is better that a person not exaggerate in extracting remote matters from the speech of God, exalted is He, adhering to the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, when, while reciting ("He frowned") [Abasa: 1], he said to himself: "We have known all of this, so what is the abb?" Then he raised a staff that was in his hand and said: "By God's life, this is the imposition; and what is it to you, O 'Umar, if you do not know what the abb is?" Then he said: "Follow what has been made clear to you of this Book, and leave what is not."  The benefit of His speech, exalted is He, will come in the interpretation of the surah, if God, exalted is He, wills.

The second answer: what we have said, namely that He mentioned in the previous surah ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ four times to explain what is in that meaning, and three times for affirmation and repetition. Among numbers, three and seven have benefits, which we mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the sea, after it, is extended by seven seas﴾ [Luqman: 27]. So when He mentioned the punishment three times, He mentioned the blessings thirty-one times: to explain what is in it of meaning, and thirty times for affirmation. The blessings are mentioned ten times more than the mentions of punishment, as a sign of the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

The third: the thirty times are repetition after the explanation in the first time, because the address is with the jinn and humans, and the blessings are confined to repelling what is disliked and attaining what is intended. But the greatest of disliked things is the punishment of Hell, ﴿it has seven gates﴾ [al-Hijr: 44], and the most complete of intended goals is the bliss of Paradise, which has eight gates. So the closing of the seven gates and the opening of the eight gates are all a blessing and honor. If you consider those blessings in relation to the two kinds, the jinn and humans, they reach thirty times, and these are the times of repetition for affirmation, while the first time explains the benefit of the speech. This is transmitted, but it is weak, because God, exalted is He, mentioned the blessings of this world and the next, while this view mentions only the blessings of the next, limiting itself to explaining them.

The fourth: the gates of the Fire are seven, and God, exalted is He, mentioned seven verses concerning warning against the Fire, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will attend to you, O you two weighty ones﴾ [al-Rahman: 31], to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will go around between it and scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned after that two gardens, when He said ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], and each garden has eight gates, all open to the God-fearing. And from the beginning of the surah up to what we have mentioned of the verses of warning, He mentioned eight times ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ — seven times for affirmation through repetition, to complete the great number which is seven. We have explained the reason for its particularity in His saying ﴿seven seas﴾, and we will repeat a part of it if God, exalted is He, wills. So the total became thirty times, the one time that comes after the many blessings to explain the meaning, which is the origin, and the multiplication being repetition, so it became thirty-one times.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. As for "ṣalṣāl" (dry clay), there are two interpretations:

The first: it means "masnūn," from ṣalla al-laḥm (the meat became foul) when it rots; in this case ṣalṣāl is from ṣulūl (putrefaction).

The second: it is from al-ṣalīl (the ringing sound). One says ṣalla al-ḥadīd ṣalīlan when a sound arises from iron. On this view, it is dry clay, whose pieces strike one another so that a sound arises between them, since it is sticky clay (ṭīn lāzib) that, when it clings to something and then separates from it all at once, makes a sound at the moment of separation.

If it is asked: man was created from ṣalṣāl, so how is it that the Qur'an says he was created from dust (turāb), and that he was created from clay (ṭīn), from black mud (ḥama'), and from a despised fluid (mā' mahīn), and so on? We say: as for His saying ﴿from dust﴾ at one place, and ﴿from a despised fluid﴾ at another, this is with regard to two persons: Adam was created from ṣalṣāl and ḥama', and his offspring were created from a despised fluid; and had Adam not been created, his offspring would not have been created. It is also permissible to say, "Zayd was created from ḥama'," meaning that his origin, who is his grandfather, was created from it. As for His saying ﴿from sticky clay﴾ and ﴿from black mud﴾ and other such expressions, it indicates that Adam, peace be upon him, was first created from dust, then became clay, then black mud shaped into form (ḥama' masnūn), then sticky clay (ṭīn lāzib); so it is as though he was created from this and from that and from that.

As for al-fakhkhār (pottery), it is clay baked by fire, namely earthenware (al-kházaf), used according to its root derivation; it is an intensive form of al-fākhir (one who boasts), like al-ʿallām (the very knowing) for al-ʿālim (the knower). This is because dust, whose nature is to crumble, when it becomes such that it is made into a vessel for water and liquids and does not crumble nor soften, it is as though it boasts over the individuals of its kind.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿وخَلَقَ الجانَّ مِن مارِجٍ مِن نارٍ﴾ ﴿فَبِأيِّ آلاءِ رَبِّكُما تُكَذِّبانِ﴾ وفي الجانِّ وجْهانِ: أحَدُهُما: هو أبُو الجِنِّ، كَما أنَّ الإنْسانَ المَذْكُورَ هُنا هو أبُو الإنْسِ وهو آدَمُ. ثانِيهِما: هو الجِنُّ بِنَفْسِهِ، فالجانُّ والجِنُّ وصْفانِ مِن بابٍ واحِدٍ، كَما يُقالُ: مِلْحٌ ومالِحٌ، أوْ نَقُولُ: الجِنُّ اسْمُ الجِنْسِ كالمِلْحِ، والجانُّ مِثْلُ الصِّفَةِ كالمالِحِ.

وفِيهِ بَحْثٌ: وهو أنَّ العَرَبَ تَقُولُ: جُنَّ الرَّجُلُ ولا يُعْلَمُ لَهُ فاعِلٌ يُبْنى الفِعْلُ مَعَهُ عَلى المَذْكُورِ، وأصْلُ ذَلِكَ: جَنَّهُ الجانُّ فَهو مَجْنُونٌ، فَلا يُذْكَرُ الفاعِلُ لِعَدَمِ العِلْمِ بِهِ، ويُقْتَصَرُ عَلى قَوْلِهِمْ: جُنَّ فَهو مَجْنُونٌ. وينبغي أنْ يُعْلَمَ أنَّ القائِلَ الأوَّلَ لا يَقُولُ: الجانُّ اسْمُ عَلَمٍ؛ لِأنَّ الجانَّ لِلْجِنِّ كَآدَمَ لَنا، وإنَّما يَقُولُ بِأنَّ المُرادَ مِنَ الجانِّ أبُوهم، كَما أنَّ المُرادَ مِنَ الإنْسانِ أبُونا آدَمُ، فالأوَّلُ مِنّا خُلِقَ مِن صَلْصالٍ، ومَن بَعْدَهُ خُلِقَ مِن صُلْبِهِ، كَذَلِكَ الجِنُّ الأوَّلُ خُلِقَ مِن نارٍ، ومَن بَعْدَهُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِهِ خُلِقَ مِن مارِجٍ، والمارِجُ: المُخْتَلِطُ. ثُمَّ فِيهِ وجْهانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّ المارِجَ هو النّارُ المَشُوبَةُ بِدُخانٍ. والثّانِي: النّارُ الصّافِيَةُ. والثّانِي أصَحُّ مِن حَيْثُ اللَّفْظِ والمَعْنى. أمّا اللَّفْظُ: فَلِأنَّهُ تَعالى قالَ: ﴿مِن مارِجٍ مِن نارٍ﴾ أيْ نارٍ مارِجَةٍ، وهَذا كَقَوْلِ القائِلِ: هو مَصُوغٌ مِن ذَهَبٍ، فَإنَّ قَوْلَهُ: مِن ذَهَبٍ فِيهِ بَيانُ تَناسُبِ الأخْلاطِ، فَيَكُونُ المَعْنى: الكُلُّ مِن ذَهَبٍ، غَيْرَ أنَّهُ يَكُونُ أنْواعًا مُخْتَلِفَةً مُخْتَلِطَةً، بِخِلافِ ما إذا قُلْتَ: هَذا قَمْحٌ مُخْتَلِطٌ، فَلَكَ أنْ تَقُولَ: مُخْتَلِطٌ بِماذا؟ فَيَقُولُ: مِن كَذا وكَذا، فَلَوِ اقْتَصَرَ عَلى قَوْلِهِ: مِن قَمْحٍ، وكانَ مِنهُ ومِن غَيْرِهِ أيْضًا، لَكانَ اقْتِصارُهُ عَلَيْهِ مُخْتَلِطًا بِما طُلِبَ مِنَ البَيانِ. وأمّا المَعْنى: فَلَأنَّهُ تَعالى كَما قالَ: ﴿خَلَقَ الإنْسانَ مِن صَلْصالٍ﴾ أيْ مِن طِينٍ حَرٍّ، كَذَلِكَ بَيَّنَ أنَّ خَلْقَ الجانِّ مِن نارٍ خالِصَةٍ. فَإنْ قِيلَ: فَكَيْفَ يَصِحُّ قَوْلُهُ: ﴿مارِجٍ﴾ بِمَعْنى مُخْتَلَطٍ مَعَ أنَّهُ خالِصٌ؟ نَقُولُ: النّارُ إذا قَوِيَتِ التَهَبَتْ، ودَخَلَ بَعْضُها في بَعْضٍ كالشَّيْءِ المُمْتَزِجِ امْتِزاجًا جَيِّدًا، لا تُمَيِّزُ فِيهِ بَيْنَ الأجْزاءِ المُخْتَلِطَةِ، وكَأنَّهُ مِن حَقِيقَةٍ واحِدَةٍ، كَما في الطِّينِ المُخْتَمِرِ، وذَلِكَ يَظْهَرُ في التَّنُّورِ المَسْجُورِ، إنْ قَرُبَ مِنهُ الحَطَبُ تَحْرِقُهُ، فَكَذَلِكَ ”مارِجٌ“ بَعْضُها بِبَعْضٍ، لا يُعْقَلُ بَيْنَ أجْزائِها دُخانٌ وأجْزاءٌ أرْضِيَّةٌ. وسَنُبَيِّنُ هَذا في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿مَرَجَ البَحْرَيْنِ﴾. فَإنْ قِيلَ: المَقْصُودُ تَعْدِيدُ النِّعَمِ عَلى الإنْسانِ، فَما وجْهُ بَيانِ خَلْقِ الجانِّ؟ نَقُولُ: الجَوابُ عَنْهُ مِن وُجُوهٍ:
