ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿بَيْنَهُما بَرْزَخٌ لا يَبْغِيانِ﴾ إشارَةً إلى ما ذَكَرْنا مِن مَنْعِهِ إيّاهُما مِنَ الجَرَيانِ عَلى عادَتِهِما، والبَرْزَخُ: الحاجِزُ، وهو قُدْرَةُ اللَّهِ تَعالى في البَعْضِ، وبِقُدْرَةِ اللَّهِ في الباقِي؛ فَإنَّ البَحْرَيْنِ قَدْ يَكُونُ بَيْنَهُما حاجِزٌ أرْضِيٌّ مَحْسُوسٌ، وقَدْ لا يَكُونُ. وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿لا يَبْغِيانِ﴾ فِيهِ وجْهانِ: أحَدُهُما: مِنَ البَغْيِ، أيْ لا يَظْلِمُ أحَدُهُما الآخَرَ، بِخِلافِ قَوْلِ الطَّبِيعِيِّ حَيْثُ يَقُولُ: الماءانِ كِلاهُما جُزْءٌ واحِدٌ، فَقالَ: هُما لا يَبْغِيانِ ذَلِكَ. وثانِيهِما: أنْ يُقالَ: لا يَبْغِيانِ مِنَ البَغْيِ بِمَعْنى الطَّلَبِ، أيْ لا يَطْلُبانِ شَيْئًا. وعَلى هَذا فَفِيهِ وجْهٌ آخَرُ، وهو أنْ يُقالَ: إنَّ ﴿يَبْغِيانِ﴾ لا مَفْعُولَ لَهُ مُعَيَّنٌ، بَلْ هو بَيانُ أنَّهُما لا يَبْغِيانِ في ذاتِهِما، ولا يَطْلُبانِ شَيْئًا أصْلًا، بِخِلافِ ما يَقُولُ الطَّبِيعِيُّ: إنَّهُ يَطْلُبُ الحَرَكَةَ والسُّكُونَ في مَوْضِعٍ عَنْ مَوْضِعٍ.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ And on this there are several issues:

First issue: Concerning the readings in which it is read yakhruju (يَخْرُجُ) from kharaja, and yukhraju (يُخْرَجُ) with a fatha on the ra' from akhraja. On both readings, al-lu'lu' (اللُّؤْلُؤُ, pearls) and al-marjan (المَرْجانِ, coral) are in the nominative case. Yukhriju with a kasra on the ra' means "Allah brings forth." And nukhriju with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the ra' is also read; on both of these readings, al-lu'lu' and al-marjan are in the accusative case. Al-lu'lu' is the large pearls, and al-marjan is their small ones. It is also said that al-marjan is the red stone.

Second issue: Pearls only come out of salt water, so how does He say ﴿from them﴾? We say the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first of them: The apparent meaning of the words of Allah the Exalted takes precedence over the words of some people whose statements are not to be trusted. And who has known that pearls do not come out of sweet water? Grant that the divers only brought them out of salt water and only found them in it; it does not follow from this that they are not found elsewhere. Suppose we accept: why do you say that the oyster comes out, by the command of Allah, from sweet water into salt water? And how can certainty be reached when the apparent earthly matters are hidden from the merchants who crossed the deserts and travelled the lands? How then could the matter of what is at the bottom of the sea be hidden from them?

The second: We say: if their statement that pearls only come out of the salt sea is correct, then we say: there are several aspects to it:

The first: The oyster produces pearl only from the rain, which is the sea of the sky.

The second: It is produced at the meeting place of the two, then the oyster enters the salt water when the pearl forms in it, seeking the saltiness, like a pregnant woman who craves saltiness at the beginning of pregnancy; it becomes heavy there, so it cannot enter the sweet water.

The third: What you mentioned would only be an objection if He had said: "It comes out of each one of them." But with His words ﴿from them﴾, there is no objection, since what comes out is from one of them, even though one of them is unspecified, and it comes out "from them," as the Exalted said: ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16]. One says: "So-and-so came out of the lands of such-and-such and entered the lands of such-and-such," and he did not come out except from one place in a house in a quarter of a town.

The fourth: "Min" (مِن, from) is not for the starting point of a thing, as one says: "I came out of Kufa," but rather for an intellectual starting point, as one says: "Adam was created from dust," and "the spirit came into being from the command of Allah." Likewise, the pearl comes out of the water, meaning it is produced from it.

Third issue: What great blessing is there in the pearl and the coral that Allah mentions them alongside the blessing of teaching the Qur'an and the creation of man? In answering this, there are two views:

The first: We say: blessings include the creation of the necessities, such as the earth which is our place, and were it not for the earth, the existence of settled life would not be possible, and likewise the provision by which there is subsistence. And among them is the creation of what is needed even if it is not a necessity, such as the kinds of grains and the running of the sun and the moon. And among them is what is beneficial even if one has no need of it, such as the kinds of fruits and the creation of the seas as part of that, as the Exalted said: ﴿and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. And among them is adornment even if it is not beneficial, such as pearls and coral, as the Exalted said: ﴿and you extract ornaments which you wear﴾ [Fatir: 12]. So Allah the Exalted mentioned the four kinds of blessings that relate to the physical faculties, and He introduced them with the great power which is the spirit, and this is knowledge, with His words: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾.

The second: We say: these are an explanation of the wonders of Allah the Exalted, not an explanation of blessings, and blessings have already been mentioned here. This is because the creation of man from clay, and the creation of the jinn from fire, are of the category of wonders, not of the category of blessings; and if Allah had created man from any other substance, it would have been a favour. Knowing this, we say: the elements are four: earth, water, air and fire. Allah the Exalted

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verse 24–25:

Then He said: ﴿And His are the ships, lofty in the sea like mountains.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: What is the benefit in making the ships exclusively His, when the heavens and what is in them, and the earth and what is upon it, are also His? We say: this speech is addressed to the common people, so He mentioned what no one who has even a little intellect can overlook, let alone the discerning and intelligent. He said: there is no doubt that the ship on the sea is not truly owned by anyone, since no one has control over this ship; rather, all of them are waiting for the mercy of God Most High, acknowledging that their wealth and their lives are in the grip of the power of God Most High. In that state they say: "To You belongs the ship, and To You belongs the dominion," and they attribute the sea and the ship to Him. Then, when they come out and look at their houses built of stone and lime, and the faces of destruction become hidden from them, they call upon the Owner of the ship, and they attribute to Him what they used to attribute to the sea and the ship. To this refers His saying: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], and so on.

The second issue: ﴿al-jawari﴾ is the plural of jariyah, and it is either a noun for the ship or an adjective. If it is a noun, it entails homonymy (ishtirak), and the original state is its absence. If it is an adjective, the original is that the adjective agrees with the thing described, and the thing described is not mentioned here. So we say: the apparent reading is that it is an adjective of that which runs (al-lati tajri). It is reported from al-Maydani that al-jariyah is the ship which runs, because it is set up for running, and the enslaved woman was called jariyah because the free woman is sought for residence and marriage, while the enslaved woman is for running about in needs; but the word came to prevail over the ship, because in most of its conditions it runs. Reason indicates what we have mentioned, that the ship is what runs; however, by way of derivation it came to prevail as a name for the running ship, and then this designation came to be applied to it even if it does not run, so that a ship at rest or moored on the sea shore is called jariyah, because it is the sort that runs; and an enslaved woman sitting is called jariyah by way of prevalence. The described thing has been omitted and the adjective has been placed in its stead. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And His are the jawari﴾, i.e., the running ships. Moreover, the word safinah is also a fa'ilah from al-safn, which means carving; it is a fa'ilah in the sense of fa'ilah according to Ibn Duraid, meaning that it carves the water, or a fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah according to others, meaning carved. So al-jariyah and al-safinah are both applied to the vessel. There is a subtle verbal point in this: when God Most High commanded Noah, peace be upon him, to make the ship, He said: ﴿And make the ark under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37]. At the beginning He called it al-fulk, because it had not yet run; then after he made it He named it safinah, as God Most High said: ﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 15], and He named it jariyah, as God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the running ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. We have known the matter of the ark and its running, and it has become like the thing named by it. So al-fulk comes before all, then al-safinah, then al-jariyah.

The third issue: What is the meaning of al-munsha'at? We say: there are two views on it. The first: the raised ones, from nasha'a al-sahabah when it rose, and anshaʾahu Allah when He raised it. In that case, either they themselves are raised in the sea, or they are the raised sails. The second: the things brought into being, from anshaʾa Allah al-makhluq, i.e., created it. If it is said: the second view is remote, because His saying ﴿in the sea like mountains﴾ is connected to al-munsha'at, so it is as if He said: "And His are the jawari which were created in the sea like mountains," and this is not appropriate. As for the first view, it is as if He said: "The jawari which were pushed in the sea like mountains," and that is good. The proof of the correctness of what we have mentioned is that you say: "The man bold in war is like a lion," and it is fine; but if you said: "The man knowledgeable in war instead of bold is like a lion," it would not be so. We say: if you reflect on what we have mentioned about al-jariyah being an adjective placed in the stead of the described thing, then creating in the sense of making does not contradict His saying ﴿in the sea like mountains﴾, because the meaning then is: "And His are the running ships in the sea like mountains," so it is a clearer demonstration of power, as if He said: "And His are the ships which run in the sea like mountains," i.e., as if they were mountains, and mountains do not run except by the power of God Most High. So al-a'lam is the plural of al-'alam, which is the mountain; as for the sail raised like the well-known flag, there is nothing wondrous in it, and the wonder in it is not like the wonder of a mountain running on water. The munsha'at may be definite, just as you say: "The good-looking man sitting is like the moon," where the connection of your saying "like the moon" is to the good-looking, not to the sitting; so it becomes a demonstration of power, since ships are like mountains, and mountains do not run except by the power of God Most High.

The fourth issue: It has been read ﴿al-munshi'at﴾ with a kasrah on the shin. In that case it is possible that His saying ﴿like the mountains﴾ stands in place of a clause, and al-jawari is definite, and definite things are not described by clauses. So we do not say: "The man like the lion came to me," nor "The man is a lion came to me." But you say: "A man like a lion came to me," and "A man who is a lion came to me." Therefore the reading with the fatha is not to be understood except as a circumstantial state (hal), and it has two aspects. The first: that you make the kaf a noun, so it is as if He said: "The jawari, the munsha'at, resembling the flags." The second: you estimate a state, "this is its likeness," as if He says: "like the flags," and it is indicated by His saying: ﴿in a wave like mountains﴾ [Hud: 42].

The fifth issue: In the plural of al-jawari, the singular of al-bahr, and the plural of al-a'lam, there is a great benefit, which is that this indicates the greatness of the sea. Had He said "in the seas," each running ship would be in a sea, so the sea would be smaller than a sea in which there are the jawari which are like mountains. But when the sea is one and in it are the jawari which are like mountains, that is a vast sea whose shore is far away, so the deliverance is by complete power.

We say: this speech is addressed to the common people, so He mentioned what no one who has even a little intellect can overlook, let alone the discerning and intelligent. Then, when they come out and look at their houses built of stone and lime, and the faces of destruction become hidden from them, they call upon the Owner of the ship, and they attribute to Him what they used to attribute to the sea and the ship. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations.

The first, and this is the sound one, is that the pronoun refers to the earth, which is understood even though it has not been mentioned. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if God were to take mankind to task for what they have earned...﴾ [Fatir: 45], and so on. According to this view the arrangement (tartib) is extremely fine. This is because when God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And His are the ships rising high upon the sea﴾, it was an indication that everyone knows and is certain that when he is on the sea, his soul, his body and his wealth are in the grip of God, exalted is He. Then when he comes out onto land and looks at the stability that the earth has and the firm footing he has upon it, he forgets his situation, so He reminded him and said: there is no difference between the two states with respect to the power of God, exalted is He, and everyone upon the surface of the earth is like the one upon the surface of the water. If the intelligent person considers carefully, the sinking of the heavy earth in the water upon which it rests is closer to reason than the sinking of the light ship in it.

The second: the pronoun refers to the ships (al-jawari), but by necessity of what precedes it, as if He, exalted is He, had said: "the ships." And there is no doubt that everyone in them is closer to passing away, so how could he deny that he is in the dominion of God, exalted is He, while in that state he possesses for himself neither benefit nor harm? God's saying: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honor﴾ indicates that the first view is the sound one. There are several issues in this:

صفحة ٩٣

The first issue: ﴿man﴾ is used for rational beings, while everything upon the surface of the earth, along with the earth, is passing away. What is the benefit of specifying rational beings? We say: the one who benefits from the warning is the rational being, so God, exalted is He, singled him out for mention.

The second issue: "the passing away one" (al-fani) is the one who has passed away. Everyone upon it will pass away, so he is still remaining and is not passing away. We say, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30], and as one says of someone near, "he has arrived." Another answer: the existence of a human being is an accident (ʿaraḍ), which is not lasting and is not remaining, so it is passing away. The affair of this world lies between two things, coming into being and non-being. As for remaining, there is no remaining for it, because remaining is continuance. It cannot be said that this supports the false doctrine that a body does not remain for two moments, as it has been said about accidents, because we say: His saying "man" in place of "ma" removes that suspicion, for I said: "whoever is upon it is passing away, having no remaining," and I did not say: "what is upon it is passing away." "Man," while being upon the earth, refers to a body in which accidents subsist, some of which is life, and accidents are not lasting. So the whole does not remain as it was, and what remains is only one of its two parts, namely the body, and the word "man" is not applied to it in the strict sense. Therefore the passing away is not "what is upon it," and "what is upon it" is not remaining.

The third issue: What is the benefit in stating that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿fani﴾ (passing away)? We say: there are several benefits in it. (Among them): encouragement to worship and devoting the brief time to obedience. (Among them): a prohibition against trusting what a person possesses, so that he does not say, when he is in blessing, that it will never depart, and thus abandon returning to God, relying on his wealth and dominion. (Among them): a command to patience if he is in harm, so that he does not disbelieve in God, relying on the thought that the matter will pass and the harm will vanish. (Among them): abandoning the taking of another as an object of worship, and a rebuke against being deceived by closeness to kings and neglecting drawing near to God, exalted is He, for their affair is near to ending, so the one close to them will soon remain in great regret, for if he dies before them he will meet God like a runaway slave, and if the king dies before him he will remain among the creatures, with everyone taking revenge on him and gloating over him, and he will be ashamed before those he used to act arrogantly toward. And if they both die together, then meeting God after death will be in the utmost difficulty. (Among them): encouragement to monotheism and abandoning shirk, both the apparent and the hidden, because the passing away one is not fit to be worshipped.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 27–28:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honour.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: The word "face" (wajh) is used to refer to the essence (dhat). The anthropomorphist (mujassim) takes "face" to mean a bodily organ, and this contradicts both reason and transmitted revelation, namely the Qur'an. This is because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88] indicates that nothing remains except the Face of God, exalted is He. According to the correct view, there is no difficulty in this, because the meaning is that nothing remains except the reality of God, or except the essence of God, and this is indeed so. But according to the view of the anthropomorphist, it follows that the hand He affirmed and the leg He spoke of would not remain. It may be said: "According to your view too, it follows that the knowledge of God and the power of God would not remain, because you have made the Face an essence, and the essence is other than the attributes. So when you say: 'Everything will perish except the reality of God,' the attributes have been excluded from it, and therefore your statement becomes a negation of the attributes." We reply: The answer to this is by reason and by transmitted proof. As for transmitted proof, that is a matter that is mentioned in another place. As for reason, it is that when someone says: "Nothing remains of so-and-so except a garment," this includes the garment and what subsists in it of colour, length and width. And if he says: "Nothing remains except its sleeve," this does not indicate the remaining of its collar or its hem. Likewise, our statement: "The essence of God, exalted is He, remains" includes His attributes. And if you say: "Nothing remains except His face in the sense of an organ," it follows that His hand would not remain.

The second issue: What is the reason for the appropriateness of using the word "face" to refer to the essence? We say: It is taken from common usage, for the "face" is used in common usage to refer to the reality of the human being. Do you not see that when a person sees the face of another, he says: "I saw him," but if he sees something other than the face, such as the hand or the leg for example, he does not say: "I saw him"? This is because a person's knowledge of the realities of things, in most matters, comes through the senses, for when a person sees something he knows from it what he did not know while it was absent, because the senses do not apprehend all of what is seen but only part of it. Then the senses perceive, and intuition (hads) judges. So when he sees something with his senses, he judges concerning it with a matter by his intuition. But in the human being's face are gathered many organs, each of which indicates a matter. So when a person sees the face of a human being, he judges concerning him with judgments that he would not have made had he not seen his face. Thus the face is more indicative of the reality of the human being and his characteristics than anything else. So the word "face" was used in its primary sense for the human being, then it was transferred to other bodies, then it was transferred to what is not a body. It is said in speech: "This is a good aspect (wajh)," and "This is a weak aspect." As for the statement of one who said that "face" derives from "confrontation" (muwajahah), as is written in some books of jurisprudence, it is worthless, since the matter is the opposite. This is because the verb derives from the verbal noun and the verbal noun from the original noun, even if by derivation. Thus "face" was first assigned to the organ, then other words were derived from it. This is known to one who is skilled in morphology (tasrif) and eloquent in literature.

The third issue: If He had said: "And there remains your Lord," or "Allah," or something else, the benefit would have been achieved without falling into the suspicion of innovation. We say: No other word could take the place of "face," and there is no wisdom in it except what God, exalted is He, has said. This is because the rest of the known names of God, exalted is He, are active participle names, such as "the Lord" (al-Rabb) and "the Creator" (al-Khaliq), and "Allah" according to some means "the One worshipped." So if He had said: "And there remains your Lord, your Lord," then our statement "your Lord" would have two meanings in usage: one is that it is said: "Something of your Lord" is every one of them; the second is that it is said: "There remains your Lord," while in the state of remaining He is your Lord, so the one being nurtured (al-marbub) at that time would be included. And likewise if He had said: "There remains the Creator and the Provider and others."

The fourth issue: What is the wisdom in the word "Lord" and in attributing the "face" to Him? And He said in another place: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and He said: ﴿Seeking the Face of God﴾ [al-Rum: 38]. We say: What is meant in the two places mentioned is worship. As for His saying: ﴿There is the Face of God﴾, it is clear, because what is mentioned there is prayer. As for His saying: ﴿Seeking the Face of God﴾, what is mentioned there is zakat. He, exalted is He, said before it: ﴿So give the kinsman his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Rum: 38], ﴿That is better for those who seek the Face of God﴾. The word "God" (Allah) indicates worship, because God is the One worshipped. What is mentioned in this place, however, is the blessings by which a human being is nurtured, so He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾.

The fifth issue: To whom is the address in His saying "your Lord" (rabbika) directed? We say: The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to everyone, as if He says: "There remains the Face of your Lord, O listener." It is also possible that the address is directed to Muhammad (ﷺ). If it is said: How then did He say: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾, addressing two persons, while He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾, addressing one? We say: With His saying: ﴿There remains the Face of your Lord﴾, there is an allusion to the perishing of every person and the remaining of God. So He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾, meaning: O listener, so do not turn towards anyone other than God, exalted is He, for everyone other than Him is perishing. The addressee often goes out of the intention in speech. For when you say to one who complains to you about the people of a place: "I will punish everyone in that place on your account," the addressee goes out of the threat, even if he is one of the people of that place. So He said: ﴿There remains the Face of your Lord﴾ to let everyone know that others are perishing. And if He had said: "The Face of your two Lords," each one would have excluded himself and his companion, the one addressed, from perishing. If you say: If He had said "There remains the Face of the Lord" without address, would it not have been more indicative of the perishing of all? We say: It seems that the address in "your Lord" is an indication of gentleness (lutf), and the remaining is an indication of subjugation (qahr), while the context is the context of explaining gentleness and enumerating blessings. So if He had said "the Lord" without address, the address would not have indicated it. And there is an established custom with the word "Lord": it is not dropped when it is attached to a pronoun. The servant says: "Our Lord, forgive us," and "My Lord, forgive me," and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 26], and ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. Where He omitted the attachment, He mentioned it with another attribute of the expression, as when He said, exalted is He: ﴿A good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba': 15], and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Peace, a word from a merciful Lord﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. The word "Lord" (rabb) may be a verbal noun meaning "nurturing" (tarbiyah); it is said: "He nurtured him (rabbahu, yurabbihi, rabban), like raba-hu, yurabbihi." It may also be a descriptive noun derived from "Lord," which is a verbal noun meaning "the one who nurtures" (al-rabb), like "medicine" for "physician," "hearing" for "faculty," "miserliness" for "miser," and similar. But it is from the pattern fa'ala (fa'ila is the root of the pattern); and in this case it is as though it is from the pattern fa'ala, yaf'alu, that is, "fa'ala" of the kind that is for the natural disposition (gharizi), as is said of "so-and-so is more knowing and more wise," so it is a descriptive noun of Him from the intransitive pattern fa'ala, in order to exclude transitivity.

The sixth issue: "Majesty" (al-Jalal) is an allusion to every attribute of the mode of negation, as when we say: "God is not a body, nor a substance, nor an accident." For this reason it is said: "He is exalted above needing, and exalted above being powerless." The verification of this is that majesty is the same as greatness (al-'azamah), except that greatness originally lies in power, while majesty lies in action. So He is great, whom no feeble intellect can encompass, so He is exalted above being encompassed by any conceivable supposition. ("And honour" [al-Ikram] is an allusion to every attribute of the mode of affirmation, as when we say: "Living, Powerful, Knowing.") As for the Hearing and the Seeing, they are of the mode of affirmation according to the People of the Sunnah, while according to the Mu'tazilah they are of the mode of negation. The attributes of the mode of negation come before the attributes of the mode of affirmation according to us, because we first find the proof, which is the world, and we say: The world is in need of something, and that thing is not like the world, so it is not created, nor needy, nor contingent. Then we affirm for it power, knowledge, and other attributes. And from here God, exalted is He, said to His servants: ﴿There is no god but God﴾ [al-Saffat: 35], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: There is no god but God." And denying divinity from other than God is denying the attributes of other than God from God. For when you say: "A body is not a god," it necessarily follows from your statement: "God is not a body." And "the Majesty and the Honour" are two attributes that are ordered upon two prior matters: majesty is ordered upon the perishing of what is other, and honour upon His remaining, exalted is He. So the Singular One remains, and He is exalted, so that His command cannot be limited by the perishing of whoever else there is and whatever else there is; and He remains, being honouring, powerful, knowing, so after their perishing He brings into existence whomever He wills. And it has been read: "Dhu al-Jalal" (ذو الجلال) and "Dhi al-Jalal" (ذي الجلال). We will mention what relates to this in the commentary on the end of the surah, God willing, exalted is He.

It is said in speech: "This is a good aspect (wajh)," and "This is a weak aspect." As for the statement of one who said that "face" derives from "confrontation" (muwajahah), as is written in some books of jurisprudence, it is worthless, since the matter is the opposite. This is because the verb derives from the verbal noun and the verbal noun from the original noun, even if by derivation. Thus "face" was first assigned to the organ, then other words were derived from it. This is known to one who is skilled in morphology (tasrif) and eloquent in literature.

The third issue: If He had said: "And there remains your Lord," or "Allah," or something else, the benefit would have been achieved without falling into the suspicion of innovation. We say: No other word could take the place of "face," and there is no wisdom in it except what God, exalted is He, has said. This is because the rest of the known names of God, exalted is He, are active participle names, such as "the Lord" (al-Rabb) and "the Creator" (al-Khaliq), and "Allah" according to some means "the One worshipped." So if He had said: "And there remains your Lord, your Lord," then our statement "your Lord" would have two meanings in usage: one is that it is said: "Something of your Lord" is every one of them; the second is that it is said: "There remains your Lord," while in the state of remaining He is your Lord, so the one being nurtured (al-marbub) at that time would be included. And likewise if He had said: "There remains the Creator and the Provider and others."

The fourth issue: What is the wisdom in the word "Lord" and in attributing the "face" to Him? And He said in another place: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and He said: ﴿Seeking the Face of God﴾ [al-Rum: 38]. We say: What is meant in the two places mentioned is worship. As for His saying: ﴿There is the Face of God﴾, it is clear, because what is mentioned there is prayer. As for His saying: ﴿Seeking the Face of God﴾, what is mentioned there is zakat. He, exalted is He, said before it: ﴿So give the kinsman his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Rum: 38], ﴿That is better for those who seek the Face of God﴾. The word "God" (Allah) indicates worship, because God is the One worshipped. What is mentioned in this place, however, is the blessings by which a human being is nurtured, so He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾.

The fifth issue: To whom is the address in His saying "your Lord" (rabbika) directed? We say: The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to everyone, as if He says: "There remains the Face of your Lord, O listener." It is also possible that the address is directed to Muhammad (ﷺ). If it is said: How then did He say: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾, addressing two persons, while He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾, addressing one? We say: With His saying: ﴿There remains the Face of your Lord﴾, there is an allusion to the perishing of every person and the remaining of God. So He said: ﴿The Face of your Lord﴾, meaning: O listener, so do not turn towards anyone other than God, exalted is He, for everyone other than Him is perishing. The addressee often goes out of the intention in speech. For when you say to one who complains to you about the people of a place: "I will punish everyone in that place on your account," the addressee goes out of the threat, even if he is one of the people of that place. So He said: ﴿There remains the Face of your Lord﴾ to let everyone know that others are perishing. And if He had said: "The Face of your two Lords," each one would have excluded himself and his companion, the one addressed, from perishing. If you say: If He had said "There remains the Face of the Lord" without address, would it not have been more indicative of the perishing of all? We say: It seems that the address in "your Lord" is an indication of gentleness (lutf), and the remaining is an indication of subjugation (qahr), while the context is the context of explaining gentleness and enumerating blessings. So if He had said "the Lord" without address, the address would not have indicated it. And there is an established custom with the word "Lord": it is not dropped when it is attached to a pronoun. The servant says: "Our Lord, forgive us," and "My Lord, forgive me," and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 26], and ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. Where He omitted the attachment, He mentioned it with another attribute of the expression, as when He said, exalted is He: ﴿A good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba': 15], and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Peace, a word from a merciful Lord﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. The word "Lord" (rabb) may be a verbal noun meaning "nurturing" (tarbiyah); it is said: "He nurtured him (rabbahu, yurabbihi, rabban), like raba-hu, yurabbihi." It may also be a descriptive noun derived from "Lord," which is a verbal noun meaning "the one who nurtures" (al-rabb), like "medicine" for "physician," "hearing" for "faculty," "miserliness" for "miser," and similar. But it is from the pattern fa'ala (fa'ila is the root of the pattern); and in this case it is as though it is from the pattern fa'ala, yaf'alu, that is, "fa'ala" of the kind that is for the natural disposition (gharizi), as is said of "so-and-so is more knowing and more wise," so it is a descriptive noun of Him from the intransitive pattern fa'ala, in order to exclude transitivity.

The sixth issue: "Majesty" (al-Jalal) is an allusion to every attribute of the mode of negation, as when we say: "God is not a body, nor a substance, nor an accident." For this reason it is said: "He is exalted above needing, and exalted above being powerless." The verification of this is that majesty is the same as greatness (al-'azamah), except that greatness originally lies in power, while majesty lies in action. So He is great, whom no feeble intellect can encompass, so He is exalted above being encompassed by any conceivable supposition. ("And honour" [al-Ikram] is an allusion to every attribute of the mode of affirmation, as when we say: "Living, Powerful, Knowing.") As for the Hearing and the Seeing, they are of the mode of affirmation according to the People of the Sunnah, while according to the Mu'tazilah they are of the mode of negation. The attributes of the mode of negation come before the attributes of the mode of affirmation according to us, because we first find the proof, which is the world, and we say: The world is in need of something, and that thing is not like the world, so it is not created, nor needy, nor contingent. Then we affirm for it power, knowledge, and other attributes. And from here God, exalted is He, said to His servants: ﴿There is no god but God﴾ [al-Saffat: 35], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: There is no god but God." And denying divinity from other than God is denying the attributes of other than God from God. For when you say: "A body is not a god," it necessarily follows from your statement: "God is not a body." And "the Majesty and the Honour" are two attributes that are ordered upon two prior matters: majesty is ordered upon the perishing of what is other, and honour upon His remaining, exalted is He. So the Singular One remains, and He is exalted, so that His command cannot be limited by the perishing of whoever else there is and whatever else there is; and He remains, being honouring, powerful, knowing, so after their perishing He brings into existence whomever He wills. And it has been read: "Dhu al-Jalal" (ذو الجلال) and "Dhi al-Jalal" (ذي الجلال). We will mention what relates to this in the commentary on the end of the surah, God willing, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 29–30:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him; every day He is in some affair.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

There are two views concerning this. The first is that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its implied sense being: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ asked. This is transmitted and rationally sound, but it involves a difficulty, namely that it leads to a contradiction. When He said ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾, this was an indication of His remaining after the passing away of those on the earth, so how can He then be asked by those who are on the earth? As for when we say that the pronoun refers to [the matters] occurring [in our day], there is no difficulty in this view. As for the sound view, we say that there are several answers to this difficulty. First, since we have explained that He is perishable in respect of Himself and does not remain except by God's preserving Him, it is valid that God be the one asked. Second, that He is asked in a metaphorical sense, not a literal one, because when all things pass away and there is no existence except by God, it is as if the creatures were supposed to be asking by the tongue of their state. Third, that His saying ﴿and there remains﴾ denotes continuity, so He remains and restores those who were on the earth, and He is then asked. The second view is that it is a new sentence (ibtida' kalam), and this is more apparent. It contains several issues:

[p. 96]

The first issue: What do the askers ask Him? We say that it admits several meanings:
First, that it is a request for bounty; everyone asks Him for mercy and what they need in their religion and their worldly life.

Second, that it is a request for information, i.e., He has the knowledge of the unseen, which none knows but Him, so everyone asks Him about the outcome of their affair and about what is good or bad for them. If it is said: Not everyone acknowledges their ignorance and God's knowledge. We say: This is a statement, in reality, from one who is ignorant. If it is from an ignorant obstinate person, then it also applies to the first meaning, for among the obstinate are those who do not acknowledge God's power, so they ask Him nothing with their tongue, though they ask Him by the tongue of their state, because it is possible for them. The first meaning indicates the perfection of power, i.e., everyone is incapable of obtaining what they need. The second meaning indicates the perfection of knowledge, i.e., everyone is ignorant of what is with God of knowable things.

Third, that this is a request for the bringing forth of a matter. His saying ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., from among the angels, they ask Him every day and say: "Our God, what shall we do, and what do You command us?" This may serve as another answer to the difficulty for the one who says that ﴿asks Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause, because He says: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾ [55:26], and the one upon it is one for whom the earth is a place and a support, and without it he cannot live. As for those among them of the earthly angels, they are within it and not upon it, and its quaking does not harm them. So when whoever is upon it passes away and God the Exalted remains, these will not pass away in that state, so they ask Him and say: "What shall we do?" and He commands them with what He commands, and they do what they are commanded. Then He says to them: "Die when I will," and they die. This is according to the view of the one who says that ﴿asks Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause, while according to the other view there is no difficulty.

The second issue: To whom does the pronoun ﴿He﴾ refer? We say: The apparent and well-known view is that it refers to God the Exalted, and there is consensus of the exegetes upon it. What supports it is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about that affair and said: "He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises whom He wills and abases whom He wills." It may also be said that it refers to a day, and ﴿every day﴾ is the time-frame of their asking, i.e., their asking occurs every day, and ﴿He is in some affair﴾ is a sentence described by which a day is characterised, and it is indefinite, as one says: "So-and-so asks me every day; it is my day of ease," i.e., he asks me on days of ease. The saying ﴿He is in some affair﴾ is a distinguishing attribute of the days in which there is an affair, as opposed to the day about which He said: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer﴾ [40:16], for on that day He is the one who asks and the one who answers, and He is not asked on that day, because it is not a day in which He is in an affair connected with the askers from among people, angels and others. Rather, they ask Him on a day in which He is in an affair connected with them, so they seek what they need or bring forth His command by what they do concerning it. If it is said: This contradicts what has come in the report, we say: There is no contradiction with his (peace be upon him) answer to the one who said: "What is this affair?" when he said: "He forgives a sin [and relieves a distress]", i.e., God the Exalted made some days marked with a mark connected to creation, namely forgiveness of sins and relief from distress. Thus God the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾ on those days that are in that affair, and He made some of them marked by there being no caller and no asker in them. And how could we not say this? For if we left every day on its generality, every day would have in it an act, a command and an affair, and that would lead to saying that [the world] is eternal and everlasting. Unless it is said: It is a general term which has been subject to specification, like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [27:23] and ﴿destroying everything﴾ [46:25].

The third issue: According to the well-known view, God the Exalted is in every day and every time in some affair, and the pen has dried up with what is to occur. We say: There are answers transmitted in the utmost excellence, so we will not withhold them, and rationally grounded answers that we mention after them. (As for the transmitted ones): Some said: What is meant is driving decrees to their appointed times. Its meaning is that the pen has dried up with what will occur in every [day and] time; when that time comes, His will is connected to the act in it, and so it comes to be. This is a good view both in wording and meaning. Others said: They are affairs He brings to light, not affairs He initiates. It is similar to the first in meaning, i.e., its ruling does not change by its being going to occur, but a time comes which God has decreed for its doing, and so what God has decreed becomes manifest in it. These two views are attributed to al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl, and Abdullah ibn Tahir answered with them. Others said: ﴿He brings the night into the day and brings the day into the night, brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾ [30:19], and He heals the sick, makes the healthy ill, exalts the humble, and humbles the exalted, and so on. This is derived from his (peace be upon him) saying: "He forgives a sin and relieves a distress." This is the best and most eloquent, since it mentions two matters, one connected to the Hereafter and the other to this world, and it puts the otherworldly before the worldly. (As for the rationally grounded ones): They are that we say this is in relation to creatures, and to those who ask Him from among the people of the heavens and the earth, because God the Exalted has decreed by what He willed, determined and established His judgment in it and enforced it. Yet what He has decreed becomes manifest every day. So we say: God has determined today the provision of so-and-so, and did not provide it yesterday. It is not possible for the knowledge of His creatures to encompass what His knowledge encompasses, so the angels ask Him every day: "Our God, on this day, in what affair, according to our view and knowledge, are You?" The second: The act is realised by two things, on the part of the agent by a specific matter, and on the part of the object in some matters, and it is not possible otherwise, and in a manner the agent chooses from among several ways:

(Example of the first): Moving what is still is not possible except by removing its stillness and bringing motion immediately after it without any interval.

(Example of the second): Making something still, for it is possible to do so while keeping the stillness in it, or while removing it immediately after without interval, or with an interval, since it is possible to remove its stillness without moving it while the body remains. Once you understand this: God the Exalted created many bodies at one time, and created in them various attributes at other times, so their bringing about is in that time and not in another time after that time. Whoever He creates poor at one time, it is not possible to create him rich at that very time while creating him poor in it. This is evident. Whoever supposes that this implies incapacity, or imagines it, is wrong, rather incapacity lies in the opposite of this; for if He created him poor at a time when He wills him to be rich, the richness would not occur in it although He willed it, so incapacity would follow from the opposite of what we said, not from what we said. Therefore each time is other than the other time, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿every day He is in some affair﴾, and this is what the exegetes mean by: He enriches the poor and impoverishes the rich, and exalts the humble and humbles the exalted, and so on with other opposites. Then know that two opposites are not confined to two different things; rather, two like things in their ruling are opposed, for they do not combine. Whoever has in him a motion towards a place at a time, it is not possible that another motion towards that same place occur in him at that same time. God's affair is not confined to impoverishing a rich person or enriching a poor person today without impoverishing or enriching him yesterday. It is not possible to combine in Zayd a richness that is yesterday with a richness that is today. So the continuous richness of the rich person, in our view, is in a matter whose state changes, and this too is among God the Exalted's affairs. Know that God the Exalted is described as: "No affair preoccupies Him from another affair." Its meaning is that one affair does not become an obstacle for Him, the Exalted, from another affair, as it does become an obstacle for us. An example: One of us, if he wants to blacken a body with dye, heats it with fire, or to whiten a body, cools it with water. Water and fire are opposites; when one of them is demanded of him and he begins it, that becomes an obstacle for him from doing the other. But that act is not an obstacle from the act itself, because blackening one body and whitening another are not mutually exclusive, and likewise heating it and blackening it with dye involve no exclusion. So the act has become an obstacle to the agent from his act, and has not become an obstacle from the act. In relation to God, whatever does not prevent the act does not prevent the agent. So God brings about from various acts what cannot be counted or enumerated in a single instant. As for what is prevented from the act, like one who blackens a body at an instant, it is not possible for him to whiten it at that same instant. Such a thing may prevent the agent, and may not prevent him, but it must prevent the agent. Blackening does not allow whitening with it. God the Exalted is not preoccupied by one affair from another affair at all, but His means prevent other means which do not prevent the agent. When you have understood this discussion, it has benefited you.

So God brings about from various acts what cannot be counted or enumerated in a single instant. As for what is prevented from the act, like one who blackens a body at an instant, it is not possible for him to whiten it at that same instant. Such a thing may prevent the agent, and may not prevent him, but it must prevent the agent. Blackening does not allow whitening with it. God the Exalted is not preoccupied by one affair from another affair at all, but His means prevent other means which do not prevent the agent. When you have understood this discussion, it has benefited you.

**[Commentary of al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, on Surah 55, verses 31–32]**

The verification (*tahqiq*) concerning His saying, ﴿Soon We shall attend to you, O you two burdens﴾ ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾: first let us mention what has been said about it, seeking blessing through the words of the scholars, and then we verify it with a clear explanation. So we say: the exegetes (*mufassirun*) differed about it, and most of them held that the meaning is "We will intend you by action." Some of them said that it came out as a threat, according to the customary usage of people. For a master says to his slave when angry: "I will attend to you," although the master may be sitting idle with nothing preventing him.

As for the verification of it, we say: the absence of leisure (*'adam al-faragh*) is an expression for the agent being engaged in an action with which he cannot bring about another action. The one who is sewing says: "I am not free to write." However, the absence of leisure may be because one of the two actions prevents the agent from the other action. It is said: "He is occupied with such-and-such instead of such-and-such," as in the saying of the speaker: "I am occupied with sewing instead of writing." The absence of leisure may also be because the action prevents the action itself, not because it prevents the agent. Like someone who moves a body at a time when it is impossible to make it still at that same time: he is not free for stillness. Yet one does not say in such a case, "I am occupied with moving instead of stillness," because in such a place, if he were not engaged in it, but there were movement in the very place not by the act of that agent, he could not make it still. So his inability to do so is only because it is impossible owing to the movement. In the first case, had he not been occupied with sewing, he would have been able to write. When you know this, the absence of leisure becomes two kinds:

One of them is with occupation, and the other is not with occupation. So we say: when God, Exalted, by His choice brought the human being into existence and kept him for a period which He willed, by pure power and will, it is not possible, with this, to annihilate him. He is then in an action that does not prevent the agent, but prevents the action. Such a case we have shown is not leisure, even if there is occupation. Then, when He has brought into existence what He willed first, and after that it is possible to annihilate and to add in an instant, then leisure is realized. But since a human being has an observation confined to the actions of himself and the actions of the children of his kind, and the absence of leisure among them is due to occupation, he supposes that God, Exalted, is at leisure. So he has imposed upon the creation that He is not at leisure, and from this follows the action, while no matter preoccupies Him from another matter. It follows that the word must be interpreted other than its meaning.

Know that this is not a different opinion from the opinion of the scholars. Rather, it is an explanation of their saying "We will intend you," except that this is clarified. Praise be to God, who guided us to the explanation without departing from the saying of the masters of the language.

Know that the original meaning of *faragh* (leisure) is emptiness. But that, if it is in a place, then it is spacious so that another may occupy it; and if it is in a time, then it is spacious for the action. So the original is that the time of the agent is free of his action and not free. But the place is visible through its emptiness in it, so the word *faragh* is applied to the emptiness of a place in such-and-such a container, while time is not visible, so its emptiness is not seen. It is said: "So-and-so is free at such-and-such a time," because so-and-so is what is seen, not the time. The original is that this time is one of the times of so-and-so, so it is possible to describe him as performing the action in it. The saying of God, Exalted, ﴿We will attend to you﴾ is a usage with regard to the original, because when a place is empty it is said "for such-and-such" and not "to such-and-such." Likewise with time. But when it was transferred to the agent and it was said, "the agent is at leisure," and at leisure he intends something else, it was said of the agent: "He finished from such-and-such to such-and-such," while with the container it is said: "He finished from such-and-such for such-and-such." So He said ﴿for you﴾ with regard to the original. This strengthens what we mentioned, that the preventer is not in relation to the agent, but in relation to the action.

As for *ayyuha*, we say: the wisdom in calling the indefinite and bringing a descriptive term after it is that the caller wishes to preserve his speech from being lost. So he first says *ya ay*, a call to an indefinite, so that everyone who hears may turn toward it and be alert to his speech, whoever intends it. Then, when the listeners have turned, he specifies the intended one, so he says *al-rajul* (the man). Two matters are obligatory in it:

One of them: with the definite article *al-* or with the demonstrative noun (*ism al-isharah*), so you say *ya ayyuha al-rajul* or *ya ayyuhadha*, not the most definite of them, which is the proper name (*'alam*), because between the indefinite that applies to every kind and the proper name that distinguishes every individual there is a great distance. The second: placing the attention-getter (*tanbih*) between it and the descriptive term, because the original for *ay* is the annexation (*idafah*), since it is in extreme indefiniteness and so needs specification (*tamyiz*). The original of specification, as we have shown, is annexation. So he placed the attention-getter between them to compensate for the annexation. It is also obligatory to delete the definite article *al-* when *ay* is present, so you do not say *ya al-rajul*, because in that there is lengthening without benefit. For by the definite article you do not add the attention that we have mentioned. So your saying *ya rajul* conveys the benefit, and there is no need for *al-*. It requires the deletion of *al-* in the case of the semantic annexation (*al-idafah al-ma'nawiyyah*), for when it conveys definiteness, keeping *al-* is a lengthening without benefit, since it combines two definites.

As for His saying, ﴿al-thaqalan﴾ (the two burdens). The well-known view is that what is meant is the jinn and the humans. There are several aspects to it:

First: they were named so because they are burdened with sins.

Second: they were named so because they are heavy upon the face of the earth. For dust, though it is fine in its creation so that the creation of Adam might be complete, did not leave its state of being heavy. As for fire, when the creation of the jinn was born from it, it became somewhat dense. So just as dust became somewhat fine, likewise fire became heavy. So they are two heavies, and so they were named thus.

Third: the heavy is one of them only, and the other was named by it because of proximity and association, as it is said: *al-'umarani* (the two 'Umars) and *al-qamarani* (the two moons), while one of them is 'Umar and one is Qamar. Or it may be that what is meant is the generality of the two present kinds. You say: "O heavy one that is such-and-such, and heavy one that is not such-and-such, and heavy (*al-thaqal*) meaning the great matter." He, peace be upon him, said: "I am leaving among you the two weighty things (*al-thaqalayn*)."

This is because when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will attend to you, O two heavy ones﴾, and we explained that He had no preoccupation, it is as if someone said: "Why is there delay, if there is no preoccupation and no obstacle there?" The second issue: al-Ma'shar (the assembly) is a great gathering. Its realization is that al-Ma'shar is the complete, abundant number beyond which there is no number, except by beginning again in it, where one repeats the units and says: eleven, twelve, twenty, thirty, that is, three tens. So al-Ma'shar is as if it were the place of the ten, which is the complete abundance.

The third issue: is this address in this world or in the Hereafter? Then God, exalted is He, said: "A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent against you both, and you will not be able to defend yourselves. So which of your Lord's bounties will you deny?" And concerning this there are several questions:

The first question: What is the connection of this verse with what precedes it? We say: if we take "O company of jinn and humankind" to be a call that will be made on the Day of Resurrection, then it is as if He, exalted is He, said: On the day "a flame of fire will be sent against you both," you will have no means of escape. If you are able to pass through, then pass through; but if we take the call to be in this world, then His saying "if you are able" indicates that there is no escape for you from God, so that you could flee before falling into the punishment, and no helper for you who could rescue you from the Fire after you have fallen into it and it has been sent upon you. It is as if He said: If you are able to flee so that you do not fall into the punishment, then flee. Then, when it becomes clear to you that there is no escape for you and that you must fall into it, then when you have fallen into it and it has been sent upon you, know that you will not be helped, and there is no deliverance for you then, because deliverance is either by repelling before falling or by lifting after it, and there is no path to either.

The second question: Why did He use the dual pronoun in His saying "against you both" (ʿalaykumā), although before it He had used the plural in His saying "if you are able" (istaṭaʿtum), and the address was to both groups? And why did He say "you will not be able to defend yourselves" (fa-lā tantaṣirān), when He had said earlier "you will not pass through except with authority" (lā tanfudhūna illā bi-sulṭān)? We say: there is a subtle point in this. His saying "if you are able" is to show their weakness and the greatness of God's dominion. He said: If you are able to pass through by your gathering and your strength, then pass through; but you are not able, because of your weakness. It has become clear when you gather and support one another, so it is even more evident when you are separated. This is a general address to each one, when he joins with all others besides him of helpers and brothers.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "will be sent against you both," it is to explain that the sending applies to the two kinds, not to each one of them individually, because not all of humankind and jinn will have the punishment and the Fire sent upon them. It is sent upon both kinds, and some of each are delivered from it by God's grace, and no one at all leaves the regions. This is confirmed by what we mentioned: He said, "You have no escape before falling, and no deliverance for you when you fall." But the absence of escape is general, while the absence of deliverance is not general. The second answer, from the standpoint of wording, is that the address is to the company, so His saying "if you are able" is addressed to "O company," and His saying "will be sent against you both" is not an address to the call itself, but an address to those present, and they are two kinds. The speech is not connected by the conjunction of "and," so that the two kinds would be addressed separately at the beginning. When the call is not explicitly stated, the dual is preferable, as in His saying, exalted is He, "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He, "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" (al-thaqalān); where He explicitly stated the call, He used the plural pronoun, and after that He said "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" where He did not explicitly state the call.

The third question: What is the shuwāẓ and what is the nuḥās? We say: the shuwāẓ is the flame of fire, and its tongue. It was said that this term is used only for that which is mixed with the smoke that comes from firewood. Apparently this is derived from the saying of the philosophers (ḥukamāʾ): when fire becomes pure it is not seen, like that which is in the furnace that is at the height of its blazing, and like that in a heated oven, where light is seen in it, and it is fire. As for the nuḥās, there are two views: one is smoke, and the second is qiṭr, which is the well-known brass among us. Furthermore, the mention of the two things after the address to the two kinds may be for the specialization of each to one of them. In that case, the light fire is for humankind, because it contradicts their substance, and the heavy brass is for the jinn, because it also contradicts their substance. For humankind is heavy and fire is light, and the jinn are light and brass is heavy. The same holds if we say that what is meant by nuḥās is smoke. It is also possible that the sending of both is in one manner for each of them, and this is the apparent and most correct view.

The fourth question: How does one who reads "nuḥāsin" with the genitive (jarr) parse it? And if one supposes that it is conjoined to "fire," then it would be "a flame of fire and [of] brass," and the flame cannot be of brass? We say: the answer to this is in two respects. The first: its implied reading is "a thing of brass," as in their saying: "I wore a sword and a spear." The second, which is the more evident: one says that the shuwāẓ does not exist except when there are, in the fire, airy and earthy parts, which is the smoke. So the shuwāẓ is composed of fire and of brass, which is the smoke. On this basis, what is sent is one single thing, not two things, except that it is compound. If it is said: on this view there is no benefit in specifying the shuwāẓ for sending, except to show that this fire is, after all, not strong enough to remove the smoke from it, we say: punishment by the fire that is not seen is worse than punishment by the fire that is seen, because of the anticipation of dread before falling into it, and the extension of the punishment. Pure fire is not seen, or is seen like light, so it has no flame and no awe. His saying, exalted is He, "So you will not be able to defend yourselves" is a negation of all kinds of defense, so neither of them can defend itself by means of the other, nor can they by means of anything else. Although the unbelievers used to say in the world: "We are a united company that is victorious" (Qamar 44), and intiṣār means being clothed in victory: it is said of one who takes vengeance that he "intaṣara" from him, as if he snatched victory from him for himself and clothed himself in it. From this same root come intiqām (retaliation), iddikhār (storing up), and iddihān (pretense). And what is said about intiṣār in the sense of "refusal to be defended": "fa-lā tantaṣirān" means "you will not refuse," and this in reality returns to what we have mentioned, because one who clothes himself with support is thereby one who refuses (to be overcome).

Then God, exalted is He, said: "A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent against you both, and you will not be able to defend yourselves. So which of your Lord's bounties will you deny?" And concerning this there are several questions:

The first question: What is the connection of this verse with what precedes it? We say: if we take "O company of jinn and humankind" to be a call that will be made on the Day of Resurrection, then it is as if He, exalted is He, said: On the day "a flame of fire will be sent against you both," you will have no means of escape. If you are able to pass through, then pass through; but if we take the call to be in this world, then His saying "if you are able" indicates that there is no escape for you from God, so that you could flee before falling into the punishment, and no helper for you who could rescue you from the Fire after you have fallen into it and it has been sent upon you. It is as if He said: If you are able to flee so that you do not fall into the punishment, then flee. Then, when it becomes clear to you that there is no escape for you and that you must fall into it, then when you have fallen into it and it has been sent upon you, know that you will not be helped, and there is no deliverance for you then, because deliverance is either by repelling before falling or by lifting after it, and there is no path to either.

The second question: Why did He use the dual pronoun in His saying "against you both" (ʿalaykumā), although before it He had used the plural in His saying "if you are able" (istaṭaʿtum), and the address was to both groups? And why did He say "you will not be able to defend yourselves" (fa-lā tantaṣirān), when He had said earlier "you will not pass through except with authority" (lā tanfudhūna illā bi-sulṭān)? We say: there is a subtle point in this. His saying "if you are able" is to show their weakness and the greatness of God's dominion. He said: If you are able to pass through by your gathering and your strength, then pass through; but you are not able, because of your weakness. It has become clear when you gather and support one another, so it is even more evident when you are separated. This is a general address to each one, when he joins with all others besides him of helpers and brothers.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "will be sent against you both," it is to explain that the sending applies to the two kinds, not to each one of them individually, because not all of humankind and jinn will have the punishment and the Fire sent upon them. It is sent upon both kinds, and some of each are delivered from it by God's grace, and no one at all leaves the regions. This is confirmed by what we mentioned: He said, "You have no escape before falling, and no deliverance for you when you fall." But the absence of escape is general, while the absence of deliverance is not general. The second answer, from the standpoint of wording, is that the address is to the company, so His saying "if you are able" is addressed to "O company," and His saying "will be sent against you both" is not an address to the call itself, but an address to those present, and they are two kinds. The speech is not connected by the conjunction of "and," so that the two kinds would be addressed separately at the beginning. When the call is not explicitly stated, the dual is preferable, as in His saying, exalted is He, "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He, "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" (al-thaqalān); where He explicitly stated the call, He used the plural pronoun, and after that He said "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?" where He did not explicitly state the call.

The third question: What is the shuwāẓ and what is the nuḥās? We say: the shuwāẓ is the flame of fire, and its tongue. It was said that this term is used only for that which is mixed with the smoke that comes from firewood. Apparently this is derived from the saying of the philosophers (ḥukamāʾ): when fire becomes pure it is not seen, like that which is in the furnace that is at the height of its blazing, and like that in a heated oven, where light is seen in it, and it is fire. As for the nuḥās, there are two views: one is smoke, and the second is qiṭr, which is the well-known brass among us. Furthermore, the mention of the two things after the address to the two kinds may be for the specialization of each to one of them. In that case, the light fire is for humankind, because it contradicts their substance, and the heavy brass is for the jinn, because it also contradicts their substance. For humankind is heavy and fire is light, and the jinn are light and brass is heavy. The same holds if we say that what is meant by nuḥās is smoke. It is also possible that the sending of both is in one manner for each of them, and this is the apparent and most correct view.

The fourth question: How does one who reads "nuḥāsin" with the genitive (jarr) parse it? And if one supposes that it is conjoined to "fire," then it would be "a flame of fire and [of] brass," and the flame cannot be of brass? We say: the answer to this is in two respects. The first: its implied reading is "a thing of brass," as in their saying: "I wore a sword and a spear." The second, which is the more evident: one says that the shuwāẓ does not exist except when there are, in the fire, airy and earthy parts, which is the smoke. So the shuwāẓ is composed of fire and of brass, which is the smoke. On this basis, what is sent is one single thing, not two things, except that it is compound. If it is said: on this view there is no benefit in specifying the shuwāẓ for sending, except to show that this fire is, after all, not strong enough to remove the smoke from it, we say: punishment by the fire that is not seen is worse than punishment by the fire that is seen, because of the anticipation of dread before falling into it, and the extension of the punishment. Pure fire is not seen, or is seen like light, so it has no flame and no awe. His saying, exalted is He, "So you will not be able to defend yourselves" is a negation of all kinds of defense, so neither of them can defend itself by means of the other, nor can they by means of anything else. Although the unbelievers used to say in the world: "We are a united company that is victorious" (Qamar 44), and intiṣār means being clothed in victory: it is said of one who takes vengeance that he "intaṣara" from him, as if he snatched victory from him for himself and clothed himself in it.
