Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verse 37–38:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the sky splits open and becomes red like rose-coloured oil⟩ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?⟩ — an indication of what is greater than the sending of the flame (shuwaz) upon mankind and the jinn. It is as if He, the Exalted, first mentioned what mankind fears, then mentioned what every being possessing perception among the jinn, mankind and the angels fears, since their places will be emptied by the splitting, and the dwellings of the jinn and mankind will be ruined. It is also possible to say: when He, the Exalted, said ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾, referring to the inhabitants of the earth, He then said ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ as an explanation of the state of the inhabitants of the heavens. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: the fa' (ف) is originally for sequence (ta'qib), in three ways:

(One): temporal sequence between two things that are not logically connected to one another, as in your saying: "Zayd sat, then 'Amr stood," in reply to someone who asks you about Zayd's sitting and 'Amr's standing, whether they were together or one after the other.

(Two): sequence in the mind (al-ta'qib al-dhihni) between two things that are connected to one another, as in your saying: "Zayd came, then 'Amr stood up, out of honour for him," since in such a case 'Amr's standing is simultaneous in time with Zayd's coming.

(Three): sequence in speech, as in your saying: "I do not fear the amir, then the king, then the sultan," as if you were saying: "I say I do not fear the amir, and I say I do not fear the king, and I say I do not fear the sultan." Having understood this, the fa' here may carry all these senses.

As for the first: the sending of the flame upon them occurs before the splitting of the heavens, and that sending is an indication of the punishment of the grave and of what happens when the criminals are driven to the gathering place, since it has come in the tafsir that the flame drives them to the gathering place, and they flee from it until they gather in one place. On this meaning, the sense is: a flame will be sent upon you both; then, when the sky splits open, there will be the painful punishment and the severe reckoning, as we shall explain, Allah willing.

As for the second: its direction is to say: ﴿A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent upon you﴾, and this will be the cause of the sky becoming red, an indication that its blaze reaches the sky and makes it like red molten iron.

As for the third: its direction is to say: when He said ﴿So you will not be able to defend yourselves﴾, that is, at the time the flame is sent upon you, He said: then when the sky splits open and becomes like molten dregs (al-muhl), which is like melted clay, how will you defend yourselves? This is an indication that the flame sent is a single blaze; or: then when the sky splits open and melts, and the earth, the atmosphere and the sky all become fire, how will you defend yourselves?

The second issue: the word (idha) may be used merely as a time adverb, may be used as a conditional, and may be used for suddenness (al-mufaja'a), though in all its uses it is an adverb of time, yet there is a difference between them.

The first: like His saying: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ ﴿and the day when it shines forth﴾ [al-Layl: 1, 2].

The second: like the saying: "If you honour me, I will honour you." Of this category is His saying: ﴿So when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. In the first, the act must necessarily be connected to the stated time, whereas in the second this is not required: if you say, "When you teach me, you will be rewarded," the reward comes after it in time, but its entitlement is established at that time, connected to it.

The third: the example of one who says: "I went out, and suddenly the caravan had arrived." But if he says: "I went out when the caravan arrived," then it is in answer to someone who asks, "When did you go out?" Having understood this, we say: in what manner is "idha" used here? We say it may bear two senses:

One of them: pure temporal adverbiality, with the fa' being for temporal sequence, since His saying ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ is an explanation of the time of the punishment, as if He said: when the sky splits open, the punishment will occur, that is, after the sending of the flame, and at the splitting of the sky it will take place.

The second of them: the conditional, and this is in the third manner, which is our statement: ﴿So you will not be able to defend yourselves﴾ at the sending of the flame; so how will you defend yourselves when the sky splits open? As if He said: when the sky splits open, do not expect any defence at all. As for taking it as suddenness, saying ﴿A flame of fire is sent upon you﴾ and then ﴿suddenly the sky has split open﴾, this is far-fetched, and it can only be understood in the second manner, that the fa' is for mental sequence.

The third issue: which of the aspects is preferred? We say: the conditional, and in that case it has two readings:

One of them: that the apodosis (jaza') is omitted altogether, so that the listener imagines after it every terrifying thing, as when one says: "When the sultan becomes angry with so-and-so, no one knows what he will do," and then perhaps pauses after his saying "when the sultan becomes angry," speaking with astonishment and bringing an indicator of the magnitude of the matter, so that the listener goes in every direction. One says: "It is as if, when the sultan becomes angry, he kills"; another says: "when the sultan becomes angry, he plunders"; and another says something other than that.

The second of them: what we have explained of the impossibility of defence. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And the day the sky is split open by clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25], up to His saying: ﴿and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26]. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: when a flame of fire and molten brass is sent upon you both, you will not defend yourselves; when the sky splits open, how will you defend yourselves? So the matter will be arduous, and it is as if He said: when the sky splits open, the matter will be arduous in the extreme. It is also possible to say: when the sky splits open, a man will encounter his deed and be reckoned his reckoning, as He said: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ up to His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with labour, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6], and so on.

* * *

The fourth issue: what is the meaning of splitting (al-inshiqaq)? We say: its reality is its melting and its ruin, as He said: ﴿The Day We fold up the sky﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104], an indication of its destruction. It is also possible to say: it splits open with the clouds, as He said: ﴿And the day the sky is split open by clouds﴾. In this there are several aspects, among them that His saying "bil-ghamam" (by the clouds) means "with the clouds," and then it would be like what we have mentioned here of cleaving and ruin.

The fifth issue: what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And it became rose-red like oil﴾? We say: the well-known view is that it becomes red at the moment; one says "a horse that is rose (warid)" when redness is attributed to the horse, and "a rose-red room (hujra warda)," meaning red in colour. We have mentioned that the blaze of the fire rises into the sky and so melts, becoming like melted brass, red. It may bear another aspect, which is to say that warda is for one occurrence of coming (al-wurud), like the single bowing (raka'a), prostration (sajda), sitting (jalsa) and standing-stillness (qa'da) from ruku', sujud, julus and qu'ud. In that case the pronoun in "kanat" (it became) is as in His saying: ﴿It was not but a single shout﴾ [Ya-Sin: 53], meaning the occurrence or the calamity; and the pronoun is feminine because the apparent noun is feminine, though the thing is masculine. Likewise here He said ﴿So it became a single warda﴾, that is, the movement by which the splitting occurs was a single rose-like occurrence, and the whole shook and was ruined at once. The movement is known from the splitting, because what is split moves and shakes. As for His saying ﴿like oil (al-dihan)﴾, there are two aspects to it:

One of them: it is the plural of duhn (oil).

The second of them: that al-dihan is the red hide (adim ahmar). If it is said: the red hide is suited to the rose, so the meaning would be: the sky became like a red hide; but what is the relation between the rose and al-dihan? We answer: the response to this is from several aspects:

The first: what is meant by al-dihan is what is meant by His saying: ﴿On the day the sky will be like molten dregs﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 8], which is the dregs of oil, and between them there is a relation, for warid is also applied to the lion, so one says "asad warid" (a rose-coloured lion), and the rose is not the bright deep red.

The second: that the comparison with oil is not in colour but in melting.

The third: that melted oil pours out in a single flow and melts all at once, whereas iron and lead do not melt completely. So the movement of oil after melting is swifter than the movement of other things. It is as if He said: its movement will be a single rose-like occurrence, like oil poured out in a pouring, not like lead, of which the finest part melts and is benefited by, while the remainder stays. Likewise iron and copper. He used the plural al-dihan on account of the greatness of the sky and the abundance of what results from its melting, owing to the differences among its parts, for the stars differ from other things.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

The first: No one will ask him about his sin, so it will not be said to him, "Are you the sinner or someone else?", nor will it be said, "Who among you is the sinner?" Rather, they will recognise him by the blackness of their faces and other signs. According to this, the pronoun in *dhanbihi* ("his sin") refers to an implicit noun explained by what follows it. Its implied sense is: no man will be asked about his sin, and no jinn (*jann*, unseen beings) will be asked, meaning about his sin.

The second: Its meaning is close to the meaning of His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. As if He says: no sinner, man or jinn, will be asked about his sin. But there is a verbal difficulty here: if the pronoun in *dhanbihi* refers to something before it, the meaning you have mentioned becomes impossible, and indeed the meaning collapses entirely. For when you say, "No single person, or human for example, will be asked about his sin," your words *"man"* and *"nor jinn"* afterward require that one verb be linked to two agents, and that is impossible. The answer to this has two aspects:

The first: Do not posit a referent for the pronoun. Instead, *ʿan dhanbihi* is treated as equivalent to an explicit noun, as if He had said: "about the sin of a sinner."

The second, which is more subtle and more worthy of acceptance: the referent of the pronoun is placed before the verb, so it is said: its implied form is, "So the sinner on that day will not be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn." There are verbal and semantic issues in this:

**The first verbal issue:** The *fa'* (*fa*) indicates sequence (*ta'qib*). It may be temporal, as if He says: "When the sky splits, the punishment will fall, so on the day it falls, they will not be asked." There is a temporal interval between the states, not a delayed one. It may also be logical, as if He says: "The punishment falls, and its attachment to them will not be delayed by the amount of time it would take for them to be asked about their sins." It may also be that He intended a discursive sequence (*al-tartib al-kalami*), as if He says: "You flee by leaving the regions of the heavens, and I say: you will not resist when the sky splits, so I say: you will not be given respite for the length of time you would be questioned."

**The second issue:** What is meant by asking? We say: the well-known view is what we have mentioned, that it will not be said to them, "Who among you is the sinner?" On this view it is a question of inquiry (*istiʿlam*). On the second interpretation, it is a question of rebuke (*tawbikh*), meaning it will not be said to him, "Why did the sinner sin?" It may also be a question of request and intercession, as a speaker says: "I ask you for the sin of so-and-so," meaning, "I ask you to pardon him." If it is said that this is faulty in several respects:

First: when the verb *su'āl* ("to ask") takes *ʿan*, it can only mean inquiry or rebuke. When it means begging (*istiʿta'*), it takes two objects directly, as in "We ask You for pardon and well-being."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 41–42:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ The connection of these verses with what precedes them, in the well-known manner, is clear and not hidden, since His words ﴿The criminals will be known﴾ are like an explanation. As for the second view, that the meaning is that no one is asked about his sin other than himself, how does He say "will be known" and "will be seized"? And according to our view, that he is not asked in the sense of a reckoning for reduction of punishment and pardon, it is likewise. There are several issues here.

The first issue: al-sima (the mark) is like al-dizya (a form of the word), and its origin is sawma, from al-sawma (a mark or sign). It may have several meanings.

One: a branding on their foreheads. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads will be branded with it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35].

Second: blackness, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿As for those whose faces have turned black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their faces will be darkened﴾ [al-Zumar: 60].

Third: dust and gloom.

The second issue: what is the reason for the singular "yu'khadhu" (will be seized) when "al-mujrimun" (the criminals) is plural, and they are the ones seized? We say there are two aspects to this.

One: that yu'khadhu is connected to His words ﴿by the forelocks﴾, as a speaker says: "Zayd was taken away."

The second: that it is connected to what yu'khadhu indicates, as if He, the Exalted, had said: "so they will be seized by the forelocks." If it is said: how is al-akhdh (seizing) transitive with the preposition bi (by), when it is transitive by itself? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿No ransom will be taken from you﴾ [al-Hadid: 15], and He said: ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 21]. We say: al-akhdh is transitive by itself, as you have explained, and with bi as well,

page 106

as in His words: ﴿Do not seize my beard or my head﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94]. But in usage there is a refinement: if the thing seized is the intended object of the seizing, the verb is directed toward it and is transitive to it without a particle; but if the intended object of the seizing is other than the physical thing seized, it is transitive to it by a particle, because since it is not the intended object, it is as though it is not truly the thing seized, and as though the verb was not transitive to it directly, so the particle is mentioned. What we have said is confirmed by the Qur'anic usage. Allah the Exalted said, regarding the staff: ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾, and He said: ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾ [al-Nisa: 102], ﴿he took the tablets﴾ [al-A'raf: 154], and so on. Since what is mentioned is the intended object of the seizing, the verb is transitive to it without a particle. And He said: ﴿Do not seize my beard or my head﴾, and He said: ﴿so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾. It is also said: "Take my hand," and "Allah took your hand," and other examples where the intended object of the seizing is other than what we have mentioned. If it is said: what is the benefit of directing the verb to other than what the first verb was directed to, and why did He say: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks﴾? We say: in it is the explanation of their punishment and the evil of their condition. We clarify this by giving an example: when a speaker says, "Zayd was struck, and then 'Amr was killed," the object in the passive form (the verb whose subject is not named, ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu) takes the place of the subject and is modelled on it; for this reason it takes the same i'rab (grammatical case endings) as it. So if yu'khadhu were not directed to something other than what yu'raf (is known) is directed to, the verb akhdh would be from 'arafa (to know), and it would be as though He said: "A knower knows the criminals, and that knower seizes them." But the criminal is known by his marks to everyone, and not everyone who knows him by his marks seizes him. Indeed, it may be said that His words ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ mean that people and angels, who need a sign to recognize them, will know them, whereas the recording angels and the stern, harsh angels will recognize them as they recognize themselves without needing a sign. In sum, His words yu'raf mean that they will be known to everyone; so if He had said yu'khadhun (they will be seized), it would be as though He had said: "so they will be seized by everyone." Likewise, when you reflect on a speaker's words, "I was preoccupied, so Zayd was struck," you know, when the verb is directed to two objects, that the one preoccupied and the one striking are different, because it is understood from it that a preoccupier preoccupied me, and a striker struck Zayd; so the striker is other than that preoccupier. But if you say, "Zayd was preoccupied, so he was struck," it does not indicate this when it is directed to one object, and even if it indicates it, it is not as evident as when it is directed to two objects. As for the explanation of the punishment: since He said ﴿so he will be seized by the forelocks﴾, He clarified the manner of the seizing and made it the intended point of the speech. Had He said "so they will be seized," the speech would be complete with that, and His words "by the forelocks" would be a benefit coming after the completion of the speech, and so would not be the intended point. But when He says "so he will be seized," there must be something the verb is connected to, and the listener awaits its occurrence; when He says "by the forelocks," this becomes the intended point. In the manner of the seizing there is a manifestation of their punishment, because seizing by the forelock itself involves humiliation and disgrace; likewise seizing by the feet. It may be objected: you have stated that transitivity by the particle bi occurs only where the seized thing is not the intended object, and now you have stated that seizing by the forelocks is the intended object. We reply: there is no contradiction between them, for seizing by the forelocks is the intended point of the speech, and the forelock was not seized for the sake of being a forelock, but in order that its owner become one who is seized. There is a difference between the intended point of the speech and the seizing itself. As for His words ﴿so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾, there are two possible meanings.

One: He combines their forelocks and their feet. On this view there are two opinions:

One: that this may happen from the direction of their backs, so that their feet are bound to their forelocks from the back, and their chests stick out.

The second: that it happens from the direction of their faces, so that their heads are on their knees and their forelocks are bound to the toes of their feet.

The second meaning: that they will be dragged along, so that some of them are seized by the forelock and some are dragged by the leg. The first is more correct and clearer.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Hell which the criminals used to deny.﴾

It is well known that there is an ellipsis here, its estimate being: it will be said to them, "This is Hell," and similar ellipses have been mentioned in several places. It is also possible to say that its meaning is: "This is the description of Hell," so the annexed noun (mudaf ilayh) has been placed in the position of the annexing noun (mudaf), and what was mentioned before is what is being pointed to. The stronger view, however, is that the speech is complete at "the forelocks and the feet," and His saying ﴿This is Hell﴾ is due to its nearness, as one says, "This is Zayd, who has arrived," when his place is near. It is as if He had said: "Hell which the criminals used to deny—this is near, not far from them." His saying ﴿which the criminals deny﴾ (present tense, yukadhdhibu) is consonant with this, because if the speech were with the ellipsis of "it will be said," He would have said to them, "This is Hell which the criminals denied" (past tense, kadhdhaba), since at this time no denier would remain. On this estimate, one would supply within it: "used to deny" (kana yukadhdhibu).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will circulate between it and a boiling, scalding water (ḥamīm ānin)﴾, it is like His saying: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], and like His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. This is because they come out and seek relief, and there appears to them from afar something liquid, which is their molten pus, so they take it to be water. They approach it as the thirsty one approaches, and they fall into it and drink from it with the thirst of camels (shurb al-hīm), but they find it hotter, so it cuts their bowels. This is like the thirsty one who, when he reaches salty water, does not investigate it or taste it, but drinks it in gulps, so it burns his heart and does not quench his thirst. His saying ﴿ḥamīm﴾ is an indication of what has been done to it of heating to boiling, and His saying ﴿ānin﴾ is an indication of what preceded it. It is as one says, "I cut it and it was cut," as if the fire had heated it so that it reached the utmost degree of heat; and water becomes ānin (at its extreme) when it reaches the ultimate limit of heat.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ There is an inquiry here, namely that these matters are not among the bounties, so how does He say, ﴿So which of the bounties﴾? We say: the answer is in two respects. The first is what we have mentioned. The second is that the intended meaning is: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord﴾ among what we pointed to at the beginning of the surah, ﴿you two deny﴾, so that you deserve these mentioned things of punishment. And likewise we say regarding His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, that they are the Gardens. Moreover, those bounties are not seen, and this is clear, because the Gardens are not visible; faith in them arises only through the unseen. Therefore the interrogative in the sense of denial is not appropriate for them in the way it is appropriate to inquire about the appearance of the heavens and the earth, the stars, the trees, the sun, the moon, and other things that are perceived and witnessed. But the Fire and the Garden are mentioned for warning and encouragement, as we have explained, that the intended meaning is: "Which of the two will you deny, so that you deserve the punishment and are deprived of the reward?"

It should be known that the last of the punishment is Hell, and the first of the levels of reward is the Garden, and after it there are further levels and increases.

The one in fear might pursue the pleasures of his soul if the pen were lifted from him. And how could it not be so? On the second view, the one in fear draws close to the one in awe, though there remains a difference between them.

"And two deserts I travelled through twice; I crossed it with the arrow, not the two arrows."

He said: he meant one desert, as indicated by the singular pronoun in "qata'tuhu" (I crossed it). This is false, because his saying "with the arrow" indicates that two deserts are meant. There is no need here for strained interpretation. There is nothing preventing Allah from giving two gardens and many other gardens. And how could there be, when He said afterward: ﴿Both having many branches﴾, and spoke of them in the dual.

The second view, which is the correct one, is that they are two gardens, and there are several explanations:

First: one is a garden for the jinn and one a garden for mankind, because the intended meaning is these two kinds.

Second: one garden for performing acts of obedience and one garden for abstaining from sins, because the legal obligation concerns these two kinds.

Third: one is a garden which is the reward, and another garden which is an addition beyond the reward. It may also be said: two gardens, one bodily (jismiyya) and the other spiritual (ruhiyya). The bodily one is for delight, and the spiritual one is for rest and comfort (rawh). This accords with His saying: ﴿Then for him is rest, sweet basil, and a garden of delight﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 89]. The single garden is so called because its trees and dwellings are connected, with no separation between them, like deserts and wastelands that have become a single garden. And the many gardens are so called because of its vastness, the variety of its trees, and the abundance of its dwellings, as if they were gardens. And it is called "two gardens" because it includes what delights both the spirit and the body. All of this refers back to a quality of praise.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But for him who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens﴾ ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

In this passage there are several subtle points (lata'if, sing. latifa).

The first: the definite article is used for the punishment of Hell (jahannam), when He said: ﴿This is Hell﴾, while the reward of the Garden is given in the indefinite form. This indicates that the levels of reward are numerous without limit, and His blessings are countless. It should be known that the last of the punishment is Hell, and the first of the levels of reward is the Garden, and after it there are further levels and increases.

The second: we have already mentioned, in explaining His saying: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45], that khawf (fear) is a kind of khashya (awe), whose cause is the humbleness of the one who fears, while khashya is a fear whose cause is the greatness of the one feared. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28], and He said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, split asunder from fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21]. That is, if the one upon whom it was sent down, who knows what was sent down, were like a great mountain in strength and height, it would split asunder from the fear of Allah because of His greatness. Likewise His saying: ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. We said that khashya indicates what we have mentioned because the word shaykh (elder) for a lord (sayyid) or a great man indicates the presence of the meaning of greatness in the root kh-sh-y. He, exalted is He, said about fear: ﴿Do not fear; We will restore it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 21], when fear weakened in Musa; and He said: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [al-Ankabut: 33]; and He said: ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ [al-Qasas: 33]; and He said: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾ [Maryam: 5]. The permutations of the root kh-w-f (fear) also indicate this, for your saying khafiya (was hidden) is close to it, and al-khafi (the hidden) has weakness in it, and al-akhyaf (one with a weak, flaccid nature) also indicates it. When this is known, Allah, exalted is He, is the one feared and the one revered, and the servant is in fear and awe before Allah. For when he looks at himself, he sees himself in utmost weakness, so he is fearful; and when he looks at the presence of Allah, he sees it in utmost greatness, so he is in awe. But the rank of the one in awe is above the rank of the one in fear. Therefore He said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾, restricting it to them, because even if they imagine themselves otherwise than they are, and assume that Allah has removed from them all the needs they are in, they do not abandon their awe of Him; rather their awe increases. As for one who fears Him because He might make him poor or strip him of his status, his fear may diminish when he feels secure from that. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But for him who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens﴾. If this is for the one who fears, what do you suppose about the one in awe?

The third: when He mentioned fear, He mentioned the standing (maqam), and at the mention of awe He mentioned His noble name, saying: ﴿Only Allah is feared﴾, and He said: ﴿You would have seen it humbled, split asunder from fear of Allah﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fear of Allah is the head of all wisdom", because he knows his Lord through His greatness, so he fears Him.

Regarding "the standing before his Lord" there are two opinions. One: "maqam rabbihi" means the station in which he stands before his Lord, which is the station of his worship, as one says: "This is the place of worship of Allah" and "this is the place of worship of the Creator", i.e., the station in which the servant worships Allah. The second: "maqam rabbihi" is the place in which Allah stands over His servants, from His saying: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], meaning Guardian and Watcher, taking from the one who truly stands over a thing, the one who guards it so that it is not absent from him. It has also been said that maqam is inserted (muqhan) and one says: "So-and-so fears the side of so-and-so", meaning he fears so-and-so. On this view the difference between the one in fear and the one in awe becomes extremely clear: the one in fear fears the standing before his Lord in front of Allah. As for the one in awe, if it were said to him: "Do what you want, for you will not be called to account nor questioned about what you do," he could not bring himself to do anything but honour. The one in fear might pursue the pleasures of his soul if the pen were lifted from him. And how could it not be so? It is said: the elect of Allah, from the awe of Allah, are occupied with a preoccupation that distracts them from eating and drinking; they stand before Allah, immersed in beholding His beauty, plunged into the seas of His majesty. On the second view, the one in fear draws close to the one in awe, though there remains a difference between them.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Abounding in branches﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ *Afnan* is the plural of *fann* (a kind, variety) or of *fanan* (a branch). It means that they have branches, or that they contain many kinds of trees and varieties of fruit. If it is asked, "Which of the two interpretations is stronger?", we say: the first, for two reasons. The first is that *afnan* as the plural of *fanan* is the well-known usage, and *funun* as the plural of *fann* is likewise; and one should not assume that *afnan* and *funun* are both plurals of *fann*. Rather, each of them is a plural with the definite article, and the forms of *fa'ala* commonly take *af'al*, while the form *fu'ul* is more common for *fa'ala*. The second is His saying, ﴿In them are two of every fruit﴾, which independently conveys the benefit mentioned. Moreover, this is more appropriate for what is stable, with no variation in mind or in existence. If it is asked, "How can the gardens be praised for having branches when the gardens of this world likewise have branches?", we say: there are two answers. The first is that gardens originally have trees, trees have branches, and branches have flowers and fruits; these are for the delight of the beholder. However, the garden of this world is for the necessity of need, whereas the garden of the Hereafter is not like this world, so in it there is only what brings pleasure, not what is needed. The roots and trunks of trees are things that are needed and that prevent a person from roaming freely in the orchard as he wishes. Thus the Garden has branches upon which are wondrous leaves and good fruits, without thick trunks. This is indicated by the fact that He, exalted is He, described the Garden only with what contains pleasure, by His saying ﴿Abounding in branches﴾, meaning the Garden is a tree with branches that is not standing on a root and stem, but rather is suspended in the air, while its people are beneath it. The second of the two answers is that the indefiniteness of *afnan* is for multiplicity or for wonder.

Then He, exalted is He, said:

﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them are two of every fruit﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

That is, in each of the two there is a flowing spring, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In it is an everflowing spring﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:12]. In each of the two there are two kinds of fruit. There are issues concerning this, some of which will be mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿In them are two gushing springs﴾ ﴿In them is fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman 55:66, 68]. Some of them are mentioned here.

The first issue: His saying ﴿Abounding in branches﴾, and ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾, and ﴿In them are two of every fruit﴾ are all descriptions of the two gardens mentioned. It is like a single statement, its meaning being: two gardens abounding in branches, in which are two flowing springs, and in which are two of every fruit. If it is asked, "What is the benefit of separating some of these from others" by His saying ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ three times, although in the mention of the punishment He did not separate two statements with it, when He said: ﴿There will be sent upon you a flame of fire and molten brass, and you will not be victorious﴾ [al-Rahman 55:35], although the sending of molten brass is different from the sending of flame; and He said: ﴿They will circulate between it and scalding water, intensely hot﴾ [al-Rahman 55:44], although scalding water is different from the blazing fire; likewise He said: ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals deny﴾, which is a complete statement, and His saying ﴿They will circulate between it and scalding water, intensely hot﴾ is another statement, and He did not separate between them with the aforementioned verse? We say: in this there is the prevalence of the aspect of mercy. For the verses of punishment He recited in a continuous succession and mentioned them as a whole, so that their mention would be shortened. The reward He mentioned little by little, because its mention is pleasing to the listener. So He spoke with separation and with the repetition of the return of the pronoun to the category, by His saying ﴿In them are two springs﴾ and ﴿In them are of every fruit﴾, because repeating the mention of the beloved is itself beloved, and lengthening with the mention of pleasures is praiseworthy.

The second issue: His saying ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾ means that in each one there is a single spring, as already explained. His saying ﴿In them are two of every fruit﴾ means: each of them is a pair; or it means: in each of them there are two kinds of fruit. It is possible that the intended meaning is similar, namely: in each of the two gardens there is a pair of every fruit, so that in both of them together there are two pairs of every fruit. This applies if we take the pronouns in *fihima* as referring to the two pairs, or we say: *min kulli fakihah* is to clarify the state of the two pairs. An example of this is when *min* enters upon something that cannot be inside a thing, as in your saying: "In the house there is a man from the East," meaning: in it there is a man from the East. It is possible that the intended meaning is: in each one of them there are two pairs. On this reading, it functions as a qualifier according to what is indicated by *min kulli fakihah*, as if He said: "In them is of every fruit," meaning: there is in them something of every fruit, and that existing thing is a pair. This is clear in cases where *min* is used with something that cannot have another existing thing within it, as in your saying: "In the house there is of every occupant." So when we say: "In them are two of every fruit," [...]. The third: when mentioning the branches, if He had said "In them are two of every fruit," it would have been appropriate, since the fruits are upon the branches. So what is the benefit of mentioning the two springs between the two matters, one of which is connected to the other? We say: the mention of the Garden proceeded according to the custom of those who live in luxury. When they enter an orchard, they do not hasten to eat the fruits but first enjoy the sight before eating. Moreover, a person in the orchard of this world does not eat until he becomes hungry and desires with a painful desire, so how much more in the Garden. So He mentioned what completes the outing, which is the greenness of the trees and the flowing of the rivers, and then He mentioned what comes after the outing, which is eating the fruits. Glory be to Him who brings the verses with the finest meanings in the clearest structures.

It is possible that the intended meaning is similar, namely: in each of the two gardens there is a pair of every fruit, so that in both of them together there are two pairs of every fruit. This applies if we take the pronouns in *fihima* as referring to the two pairs, or we say: *min kulli fakihah* is to clarify the state of the two pairs. An example of this is when *min* enters upon something that cannot be inside a thing, as in your saying: "In the house there is a man from the East," meaning: in it there is a man from the East. It is possible that the intended meaning is: in each one of them there are two pairs. On this reading, it functions as a qualifier according to what is indicated by *min kulli fakihah*, as if He said: "In them is of every fruit," meaning: there is in them something of every fruit, and that existing thing is a pair. This is clear in cases where *min* is used with something that cannot have another existing thing within it, as in your saying: "In the house there is of every occupant." So when we say: "In them are two of every fruit," [...]. The third: when mentioning the branches, if He had said "In them are two of every fruit," it would have been appropriate, since the fruits are upon the branches. So what is the benefit of mentioning the two springs between the two matters, one of which is connected to the other? We say: the mention of the Garden proceeded according to the custom of those who live in luxury. When they enter an orchard, they do not hasten to eat the fruits but first enjoy the sight before eating. Moreover, a person in the orchard of this world does not eat until he becomes hungry and desires with a painful desire, so how much more in the Garden. So He mentioned what completes the outing, which is the greenness of the trees and the flowing of the rivers, and then He mentioned what comes after the outing, which is eating the fruits. Glory be to Him who brings the verses with the finest meanings in the clearest structures.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Abounding in branches﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ *Afnan* is the plural of *fann* (a kind, variety) or of *fanan* (a branch). It means that they have branches, or that they contain many kinds of trees and varieties of fruit. If it is asked, "Which of the two interpretations is stronger?", we say: the first, for two reasons. The first is that *afnan* as the plural of *fanan* is the well-known usage, and *funun* as the plural of *fann* is likewise; and one should not assume that *afnan* and *funun* are both plurals of *fann*. Rather, each of them is a plural with the definite article, and the forms of *fa'ala* commonly take *af'al*, while the form *fu'ul* is more common for *fa'ala*. The second is His saying, ﴿In them are two of every fruit﴾, which independently conveys the benefit mentioned. Moreover, this is more appropriate for what is stable, with no variation in mind or in existence. If it is asked, "How can the gardens be praised for having branches when the gardens of this world likewise have branches?", we say: there are two answers. The first is that gardens originally have trees, trees have branches, and branches have flowers and fruits; these are for the delight of the beholder. However, the garden of this world is for the necessity of need, whereas the garden of the Hereafter is not like this world, so in it there is only what brings pleasure, not what is needed. The roots and trunks of trees are things that are needed and that prevent a person from roaming freely in the orchard as he wishes. Thus the Garden has branches upon which are wondrous leaves and good fruits, without thick trunks. This is indicated by the fact that He, exalted is He, described the Garden only with what contains pleasure, by His saying ﴿Abounding in branches﴾, meaning the Garden is a tree with branches that is not standing on a root and stem, but rather is suspended in the air, while its people are beneath it. The second of the two answers is that the indefiniteness of *afnan* is for multiplicity or for wonder.

Then He, exalted is He, said:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 54–55:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Reclining on couches whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens is within reach.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾

In this passage there are grammatical, lexical and semantic issues.

The first grammatical issue: It is well known that ﴿muttaki'in﴾ (reclining) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its referent (dhū al-ḥāl) is the one in His words ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord﴾. The governing element (ʿāmil) is what the preposition lām indicates, its implied sense being: "For them, in the state of reclining, are two gardens." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "It is possible that it is in the accusative as a form of praise (madḥ)." The difficulty with reading it as a circumstantial clause, according to those who say so, is that the garden is not theirs only during the state of reclining; rather it belongs to them in every state, for it is theirs even before entering. It is also possible to say that it is a circumstantial clause whose referent is what the word "fruit" indicates, because His words ﴿In them is every kind of fruit, in pairs﴾ indicate people who partake of them, as if He had said: "The partakers partake of them, reclining." This carries a subtle meaning, because if eating is a humble act, as with servants, attendants and slaves, then one eats standing; and if one is honoured, then if he eats to ward off hunger he eats sitting, and he does not eat reclining except the honoured one who partakes for enjoyment, who has no hunger that would make him sit to eat, and no one there who restrains him. Thus partaking of fruit is suited to reclining.

Second grammatical issue: ﴿ʿAlā furushin﴾ (upon couches) — to what verb is it attached? If it is attached to what is in ﴿muttaki'in﴾, so that it is as if He said "they recline upon couches," as one says "So-and-so reclined upon his staff, or upon his thighs," this is far-fetched, because a couch is not something one reclines upon. If it is attached to something else, then what is it? We say: it is attached to something else, its implied sense being "those who are upon couches, reclining, partake of fruit," without specifying what they recline upon. It is possible that their reclining is upon the couches, but the more evident view is what we have mentioned, so that this serves as an explanation of what is beneath them, while their whole bodies rest upon it, and it is more comfortable and more honourable for them.

Third issue: The apparent meaning is that each one has many couches, not that each one has a single couch; so for all of them there are couches upon which they are reclining.

Fourth issue, lexical: al-Istabraq is thick dībāj (brocade). Just as dībāj is an arabicised word, because the Arabs did not have it except from the non-Arabs, they used the foreign word for it, but they altered it in a way: its name in Persian is stabrak, meaning "thick," a diminutive of "stabar." They added an alif-hamza at its beginning and changed the kāf into qāf. As for the hamza, it is because the vowels of the initial letters of words in the speech of non-Arabs are not clearly expressed in many positions, so they became like a sukūn, and they therefore established a hamza in it, just as they established the hamzat al-waṣl when the first letter of a word is sukūn. Then some of them made it a hamzat waṣl and said "min istabraq," while most made it a hamzat qaṭʿ, because the first letter of the word is originally vowelled but with a faulty vowel, so they brought a hamza that removes the faulty vowel from them and enables them to make the first letter sukūn; and when vowels are equal, returning to sukūn is closer. The final letters of words are made sukūn in pause, and a vowel is not replaced by another vowel. As for the qāf, it is because if they had left the kāf, stabrak would have been confused with masjidika (your mosque) and dārika (your house), so they dropped from it the kāf which in the speech of the Arabs marks address at the end of words, and changed it to a qāf. Then there is a well-known objection: that the Qur'an was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue, and this is not Arabic. The true answer is that the word, in its origin, was not among the Arabs as a language; the intended meaning is not that it was revealed in a language which in its original form was on the tongues of the Arabs, but rather that it was revealed in a tongue whose meaning is hidden from none of the Arabs, and it did not employ any language the Arabs did not speak, which would be difficult for them to match, since their tongues would not comply with speaking it. Their inability to produce its like is therefore only due to a miracle.

Fifth issue, semantic: Reclining is among the postures that indicate soundness of body and tranquillity of heart. The one who reclines has his bodily affairs in good order and the states of his heart in good order, because the sick person lies down, or leans upon something according to what he is able to do, for rest. As for reclining in such a way that he places his palm beneath his head and his elbow on the ground and holds his sides away from the ground, that is something he cannot manage. As for one whose heart is occupied in seeking something, his movement is the movement of one who is restless.

Sixth issue: The people of tafsir said: His words ﴿whose linings are of brocade﴾ indicate the utmost of their nobility, for whatever has linings of brocade has outer surfaces better than them, and it is as if it were something the eye cannot perceive, of sundus, which is fine, soft brocade. There is another semantic aspect: the people of this world display adornment and cannot manage to make the linings like the outer surfaces, because their purpose is to display adornment and the linings are not seen; and when the cause is absent, the effect is absent. So when making the linings of brocade did not achieve their aim, which is display, they left it. In the Hereafter, the matter is built upon honour and luxury, so the linings are like the outer surfaces, and therefore He mentioned the linings.

Seventh issue: His words ﴿and the fruit of the two gardens is within reach﴾ contain an indication of their difference from the gardens of this worldly abode in three respects. The first: in this world the fruit is at the tops of the trees, and a person reclining moves away from their tops, whereas in the Hereafter he is reclining and the fruit descends to him. The second: in this world whoever is near the fruit of one tree is far from another, whereas in the Hereafter all of it is within reach at one time and in one place; and in the Hereafter, one who is settled in a garden has another garden beside him. The third: all wonders are among the special qualities of Paradise, so its trees surround them and are drawn toward them, while they remain still, contrary to what was in the world and its gardens; in this world a person moves while his object is still. Herein lies the truth: whoever does not become lazy or idle in the worship of Allah the Exalted, and strives in this world for good deeds, his affair will end in a stillness that requires no movement. So the people of Paradise, if they move, move not out of need or desire, and if they rest, they rest not for relief after fatigue. Furthermore, the friend of Allah may have this world become a model of Paradise: he remains still in his house, and his provision comes to him moving toward him, circling around him. The words of the Exalted indicate this: ﴿Every time Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 37].

Eighth issue: If the two gardens are physical, then he is always between them, with them on his right and left; he partakes of their fruits. If one of them is spiritual and the other physical, then each of them has fruits and couches befitting it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 56–57:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In them are those restraining their glances, untouched before them by man or jinn.﴾ And here there are several discussions:

The first: On the order (tartib), and it is in the utmost beauty, because at the outset He described the dwelling, which is the Garden, then He described what one enjoys in it, for whoever enters a garden first takes in the view. So He said: ﴿Both of them having branches﴾ ﴿in them are two springs﴾. Then He mentioned what is eaten of the food, so He said: ﴿in them of every fruit﴾. Then He mentioned the place of rest after eating, which is the couch (firash), then He mentioned what is on the couch with him.

The second: To what does the pronoun in ﴿fihinna﴾ ("in them") refer? We say: there are three possibilities. The first: it refers to the bounties and blessings, meaning ﴿restraining their glances﴾. The second: it refers to the couches, meaning that on the couches there are those restraining their glances; and these two are weak. As for the first, the restriction of the restrainers to being among the bounties, while the two gardens are among the bounties and the two springs and the fruits are likewise, leaves no benefit in it. As for the second, because He made the couches their container when He said: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and He returned the pronoun to them with His saying: ﴿their linings﴾ and did not say "their linings" (bata'inuhunna) in the feminine plural; so His saying ﴿fihinna﴾ would be an explanation of the pronoun, and it requires stating a benefit, because He, exalted is He, said after this again: ﴿in them are good ones﴾, and there was no mention of the couches there. So the most sound, then, is the third possibility: that the pronoun refers to the two gardens. He used the plural pronoun here and the dual in His saying ﴿in them are two springs﴾ and ﴿in them of every fruit﴾. This is because we have explained that the Garden has three considerations. The first: the interconnection of its trees and the absence of wastelands, deserts and barren lands within it; from this aspect it is as if it were one garden with nothing separating it. The second: its containing two kinds, so it is as if it were two gardens. The third: because of its vastness and the abundance of its trees, places, rivers and dwellings, it is as if it were gardens. So from one aspect it is one garden, from another two gardens, and from another gardens. Having established this, we say: the gathering of women for companionship with husbands and intimacy on the couch in one place is not possible in this world, and that is due to the narrowness of the place, or the impossibility, or as an indication of the humiliation of women, for a single man does not gather wives in one house unless they are slave-girls to whom no attention is paid; but when each one is great in soul and abundant in wealth, he does not gather them together. Know that desire in this world, just as it increases with the beauty found in spouses, also increases because of grandeur, and the circumstances of people in most matters indicate this. Having established this, we say: the houris in the Garden combine in them beauty of form, loveliness, honour, nobility and perfection, so each one has such-and-such of female and male servants, and pleasure increases because of her perfection. Therefore it is fitting that each one should have the spacious place that suits her, so the Garden, which is one in terms of connection, becomes many in terms of the separation of its dwellings. Hence He said ﴿in them﴾. As for this world, the separation of dwellings is not a sign of grandeur and pleasure, so He said ﴿in them both﴾. This is one of the subtleties.

The third: ﴿restraining their glances﴾ is an attribute of a noun that has been omitted, and the attribute was put in its place, and the noun is "women" or "spouses"; as if He had said: "in them are women restraining their glances." And in this there is a subtlety: He, exalted is He, did not mention the women except by their attributes, and did not mention a generic noun for them. So He said at times: ﴿and houris with large, lovely eyes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22], at times: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 37], and at times: ﴿restraining their glances﴾, and He did not say "women of such-and-such" for two reasons. One of them: an indication of their being secluded and veiled, so He did not mention them by a generic noun, because a generic noun reveals of the reality what the attribute does not reveal; for when you say "the moving one, the willing one, the eating one, the drinking one," its clarification by many attributes is no greater than its clarification by your saying "animal" and "human." The second of them: to magnify them, so that their beauty may increase in the eyes of those promised the Garden, for the daughters of kings are mentioned only by their attributes.

The fourth issue: ﴿restraining their glances﴾ is from qasr, which means restraint, that is, those who restrain their eyes from looking at others; or from quṣur, which is that their eyes are limited, having no longing for others. I say: the apparent meaning is that it is from qasr, since qasr is praise and quṣur is not so. It is also possible to say that it is from qasr in the sense that they have restrained their own sight, so their sight is restrained, and they are restrainers; this would be the attribution of the agent to the object. The evidence for this is that qasr is praise and quṣur is not so. On this basis there is a subtlety: He, exalted is He, said after this: ﴿secluded in pavilions﴾ [al-Rahman: 72], so they are secluded (maqsurat) and they are restrainers (qasirat). There are two aspects to this. The first: it may be said that they restrain their glances, as is the occupation of chaste women, and they restrain themselves within tents, as is the custom of women secluded for themselves in tents, and restrain their sight from roving. The second: that this is an explanation of their greatness and chastity, for a woman who has no restraint from herself and has no guardians will have a kind of lowliness in her; and when she has honourable guardians she refrains from going out and showing herself, and that indicates their greatness. When they, when going out, do not look right or left, they are chaste in themselves. So He combined an indication of their greatness in His saying ﴿secluded﴾, whom their guardians have secluded, and here their guardian is God, exalted is He, and an indication of their chastity in His saying ﴿restraining their glances﴾. Then the completeness of the subtlety is that He, exalted is He, placed mention of what indicates chastity before what indicates greatness, and mentioned ﴿restrainers﴾ in the higher of the two gardens and ﴿secluded﴾ in the lower of them. What indicates that the secluded ones point to greatness is that they are described as those kept in seclusion (mukhaddarat), not as those who seclude themselves (mutakhaddirat), as an indication that someone else secludes them, like one who pitches tents and lets down the curtain, unlike one who takes it for herself and closes her door with her own hand. We shall mention its explanation in the commentary on the verse later.

The fifth issue: ﴿restraining their glances﴾ indicates their chastity, and the beauty of the believers in their eyes, so that they love their husbands with a love that occupies them from looking at others. It also indicates modesty, because the glance (tarf) is the movement of the eyelid, and the houri does not move her eyelid nor raise her head.

The sixth issue: ﴿untouched﴾ (lam yatmithhunna). Here there are several opinions:

The first: ﴿lam yafra'hunna﴾ — no one has deflowered them.

The second: ﴿lam yujami'hunna﴾ — no one has had intercourse with them.

The third: ﴿lam yamsashunna﴾ — no one has touched them. This is closest to their state and most suitable to the description of their perfection, but the word tamth is not apparent in it. Had the intended meaning been touching, He would have used the word that is considered more pleasing, and how, when He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿and if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], and said: ﴿so keep away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], and did not express it with a word established for sexual intercourse.

If it is said: the difficulty you have mentioned remains, namely that He, exalted is He, used a metaphor for intercourse in this world with touching, as in His saying: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], according to the correct interpretation of that verse, which we shall mention, even though it is contrary to the view of our Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him; and [He used] touching in His saying: ﴿before you have touched them﴾, and did not mention touching in the Hereafter by way of metaphor. We say: He mentioned intercourse in this world by way of metaphor only because in this world it is a satisfaction of desire, and because it weakens the body and prevents worship, and at some times its ugliness is like the ugliness of drinking wine, and at other times it is like eating in excess. In the Hereafter it is free of aspects of ugliness; and how not, when wine in the Garden is counted among the pleasures, and eating and drinking in it are constant, and so on. So God, exalted is He, mentioned it in this world with a figurative word, concealed and in the utmost obscurity, by way of metaphor, to indicate its ugliness; and in the Hereafter He mentioned it with words closest to explicitness, or with an explicit word, because tamth is more indicative than jima' and wiqa', for those two derive from gathering and falling, to indicate that it is free of aspects of ugliness.

The seventh issue: What is the benefit of the word ﴿before them﴾ (qablahum)? We say: if He had said "no man or jinn has touched them," it would be a negation of touching them by a believer, and that is not the case.

The eighth issue: What is the benefit of mentioning the jinn, given that the jinn do not have intercourse? We say: that is not so; rather, the jinn have children and offspring, and the disagreement is only whether they have intercourse with humans or not. The well-known view is that they do have intercourse, for otherwise there would be no lineages or family ties in the Garden. So the intercourse of humans with them is like the intercourse of jinn, in terms of indicating its negation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verses 56–57:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In them are those restraining their glances, untouched before them by man or jinn.﴾ And here there are several discussions:

The first: On the order (tartib), and it is in the utmost beauty, because at the outset He described the dwelling, which is the Garden, then He described what one enjoys in it, for whoever enters a garden first takes in the view. So He said: ﴿Both of them having branches﴾ ﴿in them are two springs﴾. Then He mentioned what is eaten of the food, so He said: ﴿in them of every fruit﴾. Then He mentioned the place of rest after eating, which is the couch (firash), then He mentioned what is on the couch with him.

The second: To what does the pronoun in ﴿fihinna﴾ ("in them") refer? We say: there are three possibilities. The first: it refers to the bounties and blessings, meaning ﴿restraining their glances﴾. The second: it refers to the couches, meaning that on the couches there are those restraining their glances; and these two are weak. As for the first, the restriction of the restrainers to being among the bounties, while the two gardens are among the bounties and the two springs and the fruits are likewise, leaves no benefit in it. As for the second, because He made the couches their container when He said: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and He returned the pronoun to them with His saying: ﴿their linings﴾ and did not say "their linings" (bata'inuhunna) in the feminine plural; so His saying ﴿fihinna﴾ would be an explanation of the pronoun, and it requires stating a benefit, because He, exalted is He, said after this again: ﴿in them are good ones﴾, and there was no mention of the couches there. So the most sound, then, is the third possibility: that the pronoun refers to the two gardens. He used the plural pronoun here and the dual in His saying ﴿in them are two springs﴾ and ﴿in them of every fruit﴾. This is because we have explained that the Garden has three considerations. The first: the interconnection of its trees and the absence of wastelands, deserts and barren lands within it; from this aspect it is as if it were one garden with nothing separating it. The second: its containing two kinds, so it is as if it were two gardens. The third: because of its vastness and the abundance of its trees, places, rivers and dwellings, it is as if it were gardens. So from one aspect it is one garden, from another two gardens, and from another gardens. Having established this, we say: the gathering of women for companionship with husbands and intimacy on the couch in one place is not possible in this world, and that is due to the narrowness of the place, or the impossibility, or as an indication of the humiliation of women, for a single man does not gather wives in one house unless they are slave-girls to whom no attention is paid; but when each one is great in soul and abundant in wealth, he does not gather them together. Having established this, we say: the houris in the Garden combine in them beauty of form, loveliness, honour, nobility and perfection, so each one has such-and-such of female and male servants, and pleasure increases because of her perfection. Therefore it is fitting that each one should have the spacious place that suits her, so the Garden, which is one in terms of connection, becomes many in terms of the separation of its dwellings. Hence He said ﴿in them﴾. As for this world, the separation of dwellings is not a sign of grandeur and pleasure, so He said ﴿in them both﴾. This is one of the subtleties.

And in this there is a subtlety: He, exalted is He, did not mention the women except by their attributes, and did not mention a generic noun for them. So He said at times: ﴿and houris with large, lovely eyes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22], at times: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 37], and at times: ﴿restraining their glances﴾, and He did not say "women of such-and-such" for two reasons. One of them: an indication of their being secluded and veiled, so He did not mention them by a generic noun, because a generic noun reveals of the reality what the attribute does not reveal; for when you say "the moving one, the willing one, the eating one, the drinking one," its clarification by many attributes is no greater than its clarification by your saying "animal" and "human." The second of them: to magnify them, so that their beauty may increase in the eyes of those promised the Garden, for the daughters of kings are mentioned only by their attributes.

I say: the apparent meaning is that it is from qasr, since qasr is praise and quṣur is not so. It is also possible to say that it is from qasr in the sense that they have restrained their own sight, so their sight is restrained, and they are restrainers; this would be the attribution of the agent to the object. The evidence for this is that qasr is praise and quṣur is not so. Then God Most High said: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ This simile has two aspects.

The first: it is a comparison in their clarity and purity.

The second: in the fine whiteness of pearls and the redness of rubies. Coral (al-marjan) refers to small pearls, and these are far whiter and brighter than large ones. If we say that the simile is meant to explain their purity, then there is a subtle point: God's words ﴿restricting their gaze﴾ indicate their freedom from blemishes, and His words ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ indicate their purity in Paradise. Thus He began with the intelligible qualities and concluded with the sensible ones. As we have said, if the simile is meant to explain the resemblance of their bodies to rubies and coral in redness and whiteness, the same applies: He placed the description of chastity before the description of beauty. It is also not far-fetched to say that it reinforces what came before, because when they restrict their gaze, refraining from intercourse with humans and jinn, they have not been touched. They are like the ruby that is in its mine, and the coral preserved in its shell, which no hand has ever touched. We have explained once before, in God's words ﴿As if they were a hidden egg﴾ [al-Saffat: 49], that "ka'anna" (as if) when attached to the object of comparison (al-mushabbah bihi) does not convey the emphasis that it conveys when attached to the thing compared (al-mushabbah). When you say, "Zayd is like the lion" (zaydun ka-l-asad), its meaning is "Zayd resembles the lion." But when you say, "As if Zayd were the lion" (ka'anna zaydan al-asad), its meaning is "it resembles that Zayd is in fact the lion." Yet our saying "Zayd resembles the lion" contains no great exaggeration, for he resembles him in that both are animals, both are bodies, and other things. Our saying "Zayd resembles" cannot be taken literally. As for the wording: when the kaf (like) enters on the object of comparison and one says "Zayd is like the lion," the kaf exerts a verbal effect on "lion," and the verbal effect together with the semantic effect means that the lion has been acted upon until it becomes Zayd. When you say "as if Zayd were the lion," you leave "lion" in its original case-ending, so it remains in its own state and reality, and Zayd is compared to it in that state. There is no doubt that when Zayd is likened to a lion that remains in its own state, the comparison is stronger than when he is likened to a lion that has not remained in its state. Whoever says "Zayd is like the lion" lowers the lion from its rank so that Zayd equals him; whoever says "as if Zayd were the lion" raises Zayd from his rank until he equals the lion. This is a subtle refinement.

Then God Most High said: "Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?" (55:60) "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you deny?" (55:61). There are many meanings to this, to the extent that it has been said: "In the Qur'an there are three verses, each of which has a hundred meanings. The first is His saying, Most High: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you' (2:152). The second is His saying, Most High: 'And if you return, We will return' (17:8). The third is His saying, Most High: 'Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?'" Let us mention the most famous and the closest of them. As for the most famous, they are these meanings:

First: Is the reward of monotheism anything other than Paradise? That is, the reward of one who says "There is no god but Allah" is entry into Paradise.

Second: Is the reward of goodness in this world anything but goodness in the Hereafter?

Third: Is the reward of one who has done good to you in this world with favours, and in the next world with bliss, anything but that you do good to Him through worship and piety?

As for the closest meaning, it is general: the reward of everyone who does good to another is that He does good to him as well. Let us state the verification of this saying, and all the meanings return to it. We say: goodness (al-ihsan) is used in three senses.

First: establishing beauty and bringing it into existence. God Most High said: "And He shaped your forms and made them good" (40:64), and God Most High said: "Who perfected everything He created" (32:7).

Second: bringing beauty, such as making something graceful or rare, for bringing the graceful and the rare. God Most High said: "Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like of it" (6:160).

Third: one says: "So-and-so does not know how to write" or "does not know how to recite al-Fatiha," meaning he does not know them. It is apparent that the original sense of ihsan is the first two meanings, and the third is derived from them. This is not understood except through the context of usage, from which it is most likely that knowledge is intended. Knowing this, we say: it is possible to take ihsan in both places in one shared meaning of the two meanings, and it is possible to take it in two different meanings.

As for the first: we say, "Is the reward of goodness" — that is, is the reward of one who performs a good act anything but that he is given a good act in return? However, the good act of the servant is not everything he considers good; rather, goodness is what God has deemed good from him. For the wicked person may regard wickedness as good, yet it is not good; rather, the good is what God has demanded from him. Likewise, the good from God is everything He brings that the servant seeks, just as the servant has done what God demanded of him. To this points His saying: "Therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in" (43:71), and His saying: "Therein they will abide, [in] what their souls desire" (21:102), and He said: "For those who have done good is the best [reward]" (10:26), meaning what is good in their estimation.

As for the second: we say, "Is the reward of one who established goodness in his deed in this world anything but that God establishes goodness in him and in his states in both abodes, and vice versa? Is the reward of one who established goodness in us, in our forms and in our states, anything but that we also establish goodness in him?" But establishing goodness in God Most High is impossible, so establishing goodness in our own selves and actions: we make our selves good by worshipping the Presence of God Most High, our actions good by turning toward Him, and the states of our inner selves by knowing Him Most High. To this the allusion returns. It is also reported in the traditions that the faces of believers are beautiful and the faces of unbelievers are ugly.

As for the third aspect, which is taking it in both meanings: it is that you say, "the reward of one who performs a good act is that God establishes goodness in it and in all his states, so He makes his face good and his state good." Then in it there are subtleties:

The first subtlety: this is an indication of the lifting of obligation (taklif) from the common folk in the Hereafter, and the directing of obligation upon the elite therein. As for the first: since God said, "Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?", and there is no doubt that the believer is rewarded with Paradise, so goodness from God is his reward; and one who rewards a servant for his deed does not command him to thank him. Also, if obligation remained in the Hereafter, then if the servant neglected the performance of obligation he would deserve punishment, and punishment is the withholding of goodness. Because the servant, having worshipped God in this world for as long as he remained, it befits His generosity, Most High, to do good to him in the Hereafter for as long as he remains, so there is no punishment for neglecting it without obligation.

As for the second: you say, the particular characteristic of God Most High: we worshipped God Most High in this world for blessings that He had previously bestowed upon us. So this One who gave us, Most High, the beginning of a blessing and fresh goodness has a right over us to be thanked. So they say, "Praise be to God," and they mention God and extol Him, so the very goodness from God Most High toward them becomes a cause for their performance of His thanks. Then they present to themselves His worship, Most High, so for them even the slightest worship becomes an absorbing occupation, diverting them from the maidens, the palaces, eating and drinking. So they do not eat, drink, jest, or play, and their state becomes like the state of the angels in this day of ours, who neither marry nor play. That is not an obligation like these burdensome obligations; rather, it is a pleasure exceeding every pleasure in other things.

The second subtlety: this verse indicates that the servant is given free rein (muhakkam) in the Hereafter, as God Most High said: "For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for" (36:57). This is because we have explained that goodness is bringing what is good in the estimation of the one who does good. But when God demanded worship from us, He demanded as He willed, and the believer brought it as it was demanded of him, so he became a doer of good. This requires that God do good to His servant and bring what is good in his estimation, which is what he seeks, as He wills. So it is as if He said: "Is the reward of goodness" — that is, is the reward of one who brought what I demanded from him according to My will anything but that he be brought what he demanded from Me according to his will? But will is connected with seeing, so by the judgment of the promise it must be that this verse is a sign indicating the seeing [of God] with the eye (al-ru'yah al-bal-kafiyyah).

The third subtlety: this verse indicates that every kind of goodness that a human conceives of from God Most High is less than the goodness that God Most High has promised, because when a generous man says to a poor man, "Do such-and-such and you will have such-and-such a dinar," and says to another, "Do such-and-such on condition that I do good to you," the hope of one for whom no specific reward is designated is greater than the hope of one for whom it is designated. This is when the generous man is at the utmost of generosity and the pinnacle of wealth. If this is established, then God Most High said: the reward of one who does good to Me is that I do good to him in a way that makes him envied, and I bring to him beyond what he desires. So what God gives beyond what one hopes for is in accordance with His generosity and bounty.
