But establishing goodness in God Most High is impossible, so establishing goodness in our own selves and actions: we make our selves good by worshipping the Presence of God Most High, our actions good by turning toward Him, and the states of our inner selves by knowing Him Most High. To this the allusion returns. It is also reported in the traditions that the faces of believers are beautiful and the faces of unbelievers are ugly.

As for the third aspect, which is taking it in both meanings: it is that you say, "the reward of one who performs a good act is that God establishes goodness in it and in all his states, so He makes his face good and his state good." Then in it there are subtleties:

The first subtlety: this is an indication of the lifting of obligation (taklif) from the common folk in the Hereafter, and the directing of obligation upon the elite therein. As for the first: since God said, "Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?", and there is no doubt that the believer is rewarded with Paradise, so goodness from God is his reward; and one who rewards a servant for his deed does not command him to thank him. Also, if obligation remained in the Hereafter, then if the servant neglected the performance of obligation he would deserve punishment, and punishment is the withholding of goodness. Because the servant, having worshipped God in this world for as long as he remained, it befits His generosity, Most High, to do good to him in the Hereafter for as long as he remains, so there is no punishment for neglecting it without obligation.

As for the second: you say, the particular characteristic of God Most High: we worshipped God Most High in this world for blessings that He had previously bestowed upon us. So this One who gave us, Most High, the beginning of a blessing and fresh goodness has a right over us to be thanked. So they say, "Praise be to God," and they mention God and extol Him, so the very goodness from God Most High toward them becomes a cause for their performance of His thanks. Then they present to themselves His worship, Most High, so for them even the slightest worship becomes an absorbing occupation, diverting them from the maidens, the palaces, eating and drinking. So they do not eat, drink, jest, or play, and their state becomes like the state of the angels in this day of ours, who neither marry nor play. That is not an obligation like these burdensome obligations; rather, it is a pleasure exceeding every pleasure in other things.

The second subtlety: this verse indicates that the servant is given free rein (muhakkam) in the Hereafter, as God Most High said: "For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for" (36:57). This is because we have explained that goodness is bringing what is good in the estimation of the one who does good. But when God demanded worship from us, He demanded as He willed, and the believer brought it as it was demanded of him, so he became a doer of good. This requires that God do good to His servant and bring what is good in his estimation, which is what he seeks, as He wills. So it is as if He said: "Is the reward of goodness" — that is, is the reward of one who brought what I demanded from him according to My will anything but that he be brought what he demanded from Me according to his will? But will is connected with seeing, so by the judgment of the promise it must be that this verse is a sign indicating the seeing [of God] with the eye (al-ru'yah al-bal-kafiyyah).

The third subtlety: this verse indicates that every kind of goodness that a human conceives of from God Most High is less than the goodness that God Most High has promised, because when a generous man says to a poor man, "Do such-and-such and you will have such-and-such a dinar," and says to another, "Do such-and-such on condition that I do good to you," the hope of one for whom no specific reward is designated is greater than the hope of one for whom it is designated. This is when the generous man is at the utmost of generosity and the pinnacle of wealth. If this is established, then God Most High said: the reward of one who does good to Me is that I do good to him in a way that makes him envied, and I bring to him beyond what he desires. So what God gives beyond what one hopes for is in accordance with His generosity and bounty.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And beneath these two are two other gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ When He mentioned the reward, He then mentioned after it its like, which is two other gardens. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For those who have done good is the best [reward] and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. As for His saying ﴿beneath these two﴾, there are two possible meanings. The first: "beneath them" in rank, which is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) chose, and he said: His saying ﴿dark green﴾ alongside His saying about the first two, ﴿having branches﴾, and His saying about these two, ﴿two fountains gushing forth﴾, alongside His saying about the first two, ﴿two flowing fountains﴾, because gushing (al-nadkh) is less than flowing (al-jary). And His saying about the first two, ﴿of every fruit, two kinds﴾, alongside His saying about these two, ﴿fruit, date palms and pomegranates﴾; and His saying about the first two, ﴿couches lined with brocade﴾, where He omitted mention of the outer layers because of their loftiness and elevation and because minds cannot grasp them, is evidence for this, alongside His saying about these two, ﴿green cushions﴾ [al-Rahman: 76]. One may say: this is weak, because God's gifts in the Hereafter are continuous, and whenever He gives one thing after another, the one receiving it thinks that it is that thing or something better than it. This objection can be answered, in confirmation of what al-Zamakhshari chose, by saying that the two gardens beneath the first two are for their descendants whom God joined to them, and for their followers. But He only made them for them as a blessing upon them; that is, "these two other gardens are for you, dwell in them whomever you wish." The second: that what is meant by "beneath them" is in place, as though they are in two gardens and look down from above upon two other gardens beneath them. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Upon them are lofty chambers built upon lofty chambers﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], and the passage. The lofty chambers have branches near them, and the chambers below them have land that is green. On this view, there are subtleties in the verses:

The first: He said of the first two, ﴿having branches﴾, and said of these two, ﴿dark green﴾, meaning "very green, in the extreme of greenness." Idhdhamma al-shay' means it became black, but it is not used for some things. When land becomes extremely green, it inclines toward black. It may be said that land empty of crops is called "whiteness" (bayad), and when it is cultivated it is called "blackness of the land" (sawad al-ard), as one says "the blackness of the town" (sawad al-balad). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Adhere to the great majority (al-sawad al-a'zam), and whoever increases the numbers of a people is one of them." The verification of this is that the beginning of colours is whiteness and their end is blackness, for white accepts every colour, while black accepts none of the colours. For this reason, "kafir" (disbeliever) is applied to black, and it is not applied to any other colour. Since the land empty of crops is characterised by whiteness and the land that is cultivated by blackness, this indicates that these two are beneath the first two in place. So when they look at what is above them, they see the branches shading them, and when they look at what is beneath them, they see the land green.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth﴾, meaning two fountains spouting, whose water moves upward. As for the two fountains mentioned earlier, they flow toward the side of the believers. Both of them move toward the place of the people of faith. As for the saying of the author of al-Kashshaf, "gushing is less than flowing," it is not necessarily so, since flowing may be gentle while gushing is strong and abundant. Rather, what is meant is that gushing involves movement upward, while the fountains are in the place of the believers, so the movement of the water is toward them. The first two fountains are in their place, so the movement of their water toward the side of the believers is by flowing.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Reclining on green cushions (rafraf) and beautiful carpets (abqariyy)﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the wisdom in delaying the mention of their reclining from the mention of their wives in this place, although He had mentioned their reclining before the mention of their wives in the two earlier gardens, where He said: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], then He said: ﴿restraining their gaze﴾, and here He said: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful ones﴾, then He said: ﴿reclining﴾? The answer to this is from two aspects. One of them: the people of Paradise have no weariness or movement; they are at ease perpetually. But people in this world are of various kinds: among them is one who has intercourse with his wife in abundant measure, and at the completion of his need he uses washing and disperses on the earth to earn; and among them is one who is hesitant in seeking gain, and upon obtaining it he returns to his wife and relieves his heart of fatigue before fulfilling his need, so fatigue is necessary either before or after the fulfilment of need. God, exalted is He, said in describing the people of Paradise: reclining both before intercourse with their spouses and after intercourse likewise, so that it is known that they are always in tranquillity, and have no fatigue, neither before intercourse nor after intercourse. The second aspect: we have explained in the two preceding aspects that the two earlier gardens are for the people of Paradise who struggled (jahadu) and the later two are for their descendants who were joined to them; so they and their wives are in the tents, awaiting the arrival of their husbands. When the believer enters his garden which is his abode, he reclines upon the couches and his beautiful wives are moved to him. So their being in the two earlier gardens comes after their reclining on the couches; and as for their being in the two later gardens, that is achieved in our day, while the believer's reclining is not achieved in our day. Thus He mentioned their being in them here and delayed it there. ﴿Reclining﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and its governing element is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾, and this is in the force of an exception, as if He had said: none has touched them except the believers, for they touch them while reclining. What we mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ applies here.

The second issue: rafraf may either derive from raffa al-zar'u, when the crop reached its freshness, in which case it is fitting with His saying: ﴿dark green﴾, and the sense would be that they recline upon meadows and on abqariyy garments; or it may derive from rafrafat al-tair, which is its hovering in the air around what it intends to descend upon, in which case the meaning is that they are upon raised spreads, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and raised couches﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 34]. This indicates that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And besides these two are two gardens﴾ means that they are lower in place than those whose couches are raised. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿green﴾ is a plural form, so rafraf is a plural as a noun of genus, and its singular is rafrafah, like handhalah. The plurality in muttaki'in indicates it, for when He said: ﴿reclining﴾ it showed that they are upon rafarif.

The third issue: what is the difference between furush (couches) and rafraf, such that He did not say rafarif, relying on what His saying "reclining" indicates, but said furush and did not rely on what that indicates? We say: the plural of the quadriliteral is heavier than the plural of the triliteral, and for this reason there came for the plural of the quadriliteral only one pattern, whereas the plural patterns of the triliteral are many. It has been read: ''upon green rafarif'', and ''rafarif khiʻar'' and ''abaqir''.

The fourth issue: if we say that rafraf is the spreads, what is the benefit of "green", since He, exalted is He, described the garments of Paradise as green, saying: ﴿green garments of fine silk﴾ [al-Insan: 21]? We say: people's inclination towards the green colour in this world is greater, and the cause of their inclination to it is that the colours which are thought to be the origins of colours are seven: the transparent, which is that which does not prevent the passage of sight through it and does not conceal what is behind it, such as glass, clear water and others; then white after it; then yellow; then red; then green; then blue; then black. The more apparent view is that the primary colours are three: white and black, between which lies the utmost difference, and red which is intermediate between white and black, for blood was created with the intermediate colour; if health is not as it should be, then if the coldness in it is excessive it becomes white, and if the heat in it is excessive it becomes black. But from these three the other colours arise: white mixed with red produces yellow, as is shown by mixing white milk with blood and other red things; when white is mixed with black the colour blue arises, as is shown by mixing ground plaster with charcoal; when red is mixed with black blue also arises, but it is more inclined towards black; and when yellow is mixed with blue green arises from yellow and blue. It is known that yellow comes from white and red, and blue from white, black and red and black; so green has in it the three primary colours, and therefore the human inclination towards it is because it comprises the primary colours. But this is very far-fetched. The closer view is that white dazzles the sight, and for this reason a person cannot keep looking at the earth when it is covered with snow; and it produces the condition of ... and black gathers the sight, for which reason a person dislikes looking at it and at red things such as blood. Green, since these three qualities are combined in it, one of them repels the harm of another, and it produces the mixed colour found in the human body, namely red, white, yellow and black. And since the soul's inclination in this world is towards green, God, exalted is He, mentioned in the Hereafter what accords with its nature in this world.

The fifth issue: abqariyy is ascribed to Abqar, which for the Arabs is a place among the dwelling-places of the jinn; so garments made with excellent craftsmanship they call abqariyyat, in exaggeration of their beauty, as if they were not the work of humankind. It is also used for things other than garments, so that one says of a man who performs a marvellous deed: he is abqariyy, that is, from that land. The Prophet ﷺ said in the dream he saw: "I did not see anyone among the people abqariyy who makes his deed (yafri farhu)" and he dispensed with mentioning the plural by the collective noun, and described him with what plurals are described with, saying "hisan" (beautiful). This is because we have explained that the plural of the quadriliteral is somewhat heavy. As for one who reads "abaqiriyy", he has made the name of that place abaqir; if he claims it is its plural, he has erred; and if he takes abqariyy as the plural and then forms the nisbah, he has committed an artificiality contrary to what the men of letters required, for when they form a nisbah from a plural they return it to the singular; and this reader has laboured over the singular, returning it to the plural and then ascribing it, for among the Arabs there is no land in existence entirely named abqar so that it might be pluralised and said abaqir. This is the artificiality of pluralising what has no plural, and then ascribing it to that plural; and the men of letters dislike pluralising what is ascribed, lest they combine plurality and nisbah.

When the believer enters his garden which is his abode, he reclines upon the couches and his beautiful wives are moved to him. So their being in the two earlier gardens comes after their reclining on the couches; and as for their being in the two later gardens, that is achieved in our day, while the believer's reclining is not achieved in our day. Thus He mentioned their being in them here and delayed it there. ﴿Reclining﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and its governing element is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾, and this is in the force of an exception, as if He had said: none has touched them except the believers, for they touch them while reclining. What we mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿reclining on couches﴾ applies here.

The second issue: rafraf may either derive from raffa al-zar'u, when the crop reached its freshness, in which case it is fitting with His saying: ﴿dark green﴾, and the sense would be that they recline upon meadows and on abqariyy garments; or it may derive from rafrafat al-tair, which is its hovering in the air around what it intends to descend upon, in which case the meaning is that they are upon raised spreads, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and raised couches﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 34]. This indicates that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And besides these two are two gardens﴾ means that they are lower in place than those whose couches are raised. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿green﴾ is a plural form, so rafraf is a plural as a noun of genus, and its singular is rafrafah, like handhalah. The plurality in muttaki'in indicates it, for when He said: ﴿reclining﴾ it showed that they are upon rafarif.

The third issue: what is the difference between furush (couches) and rafraf, such that He did not say rafarif, relying on what His saying "reclining" indicates, but said furush and did not rely on what that indicates? We say: the plural of the quadriliteral is heavier than the plural of the triliteral, and for this reason there came for the plural of the quadriliteral only one pattern, whereas the plural patterns of the triliteral are many. It has been read: ''upon green rafarif'', and ''rafarif khiʻar'' and ''abaqir''.

The fourth issue: if we say that rafraf is the spreads, what is the benefit of "green", since He, exalted is He, described the garments of Paradise as green, saying: ﴿green garments of fine silk﴾ [al-Insan: 21]? We say: people's inclination towards the green colour in this world is greater, and the cause of their inclination to it is that the colours which are thought to be the origins of colours are seven: the transparent, which is that which does not prevent the passage of sight through it and does not conceal what is behind it, such as glass, clear water and others; then white after it; then yellow; then red; then green; then blue; then black. The more apparent view is that the primary colours are three: white and black, between which lies the utmost difference, and red which is intermediate between white and black, for blood was created with the intermediate colour; if health is not as it should be, then if the coldness in it is excessive it becomes white, and if the heat in it is excessive it becomes black. But from these three the other colours arise: white mixed with red produces yellow, as is shown by mixing white milk with blood and other red things; when white is mixed with black the colour blue arises, as is shown by mixing ground plaster with charcoal; when red is mixed with black blue also arises, but it is more inclined towards black; and when yellow is mixed with blue green arises from yellow and blue. It is known that yellow comes from white and red, and blue from white, black and red and black; so green has in it the three primary colours, and therefore the human inclination towards it is because it comprises the primary colours. But this is very far-fetched. The closer view is that white dazzles the sight, and for this reason a person cannot keep looking at the earth when it is covered with snow; and it produces the condition of ... and black gathers the sight, for which reason a person dislikes looking at it and at red things such as blood. Green, since these three qualities are combined in it, one of them repels the harm of another, and it produces the mixed colour found in the human body, namely red, white, yellow and black. And since the soul's inclination in this world is towards green, God, exalted is He, mentioned in the Hereafter what accords with its nature in this world.

The fifth issue: abqariyy is ascribed to Abqar, which for the Arabs is a place among the dwelling-places of the jinn; so garments made with excellent craftsmanship they call abqariyyat, in exaggeration of their beauty, as if they were not the work of humankind. It is also used for things other than garments, so that one says of a man who performs a marvellous deed: he is abqariyy, that is, from that land. The Prophet ﷺ said in the dream he saw: "I did not see anyone among the people abqariyy who makes his deed (yafri farhu)" and he dispensed with mentioning the plural by the collective noun, and described him with what plurals are described with, saying "hisan" (beautiful). This is because we have explained that the plural of the quadriliteral is somewhat heavy. As for one who reads "abaqiriyy", he has made the name of that place abaqir; if he claims it is its plural, he has erred; and if he takes abqariyy as the plural and then forms the nisbah, he has committed an artificiality contrary to what the men of letters required, for when they form a nisbah from a plural they return it to the singular; and this reader has laboured over the singular, returning it to the plural and then ascribing it, for among the Arabs there is no land in existence entirely named abqar so that it might be pluralised and said abaqir. This is the artificiality of pluralising what has no plural, and then ascribing it to that plural; and the men of letters dislike pluralising what is ascribed, lest they combine plurality and nisbah.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 55, verse 68–77:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are two kinds of every fruit.﴾ That is because fruit is of two kinds: terrestrial (ardiyyah), such as watermelon and other cultivated produce of the earth, and arboreal (shajariyyah), such as the date palm and other tree-born fruit. He said: ﴿dark green﴾ (mudhammatan), with the kinds of greenery, among which are the terrestrial fruits, and therein are also the arboreal fruits. He mentioned from them two kinds, namely the pomegranate and the ripe date (rutab), because they are opposites: one of them is sweet and the other is not sweet. Likewise, one of them is hot and the other cold; one of them is a fruit and a food, and the other is a fruit; one of them is from the fruits of hot lands and the other from the fruits of cold lands; one of them has trees that are extremely tall and the other has trees that are the opposite; and one of them has its edible part exposed while what is not eaten is hidden, and the other is the reverse. They are thus like two opposites, and the indication of the two extremes includes the indication of what lies between them, as He said: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], and we have already mentioned this.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful ones (khayrat hisan)﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ meaning: within them is goodness, and outwardly is beauty. Khayrat is the plural of khayrah. We have already explained that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿restraining their gaze﴾ up to His saying: ﴿as if they were﴾ there is an indication of their being beautiful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Houris, secluded in pavilions﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾

This is an indication of their dignity, for they are not confined as prisoners; rather, it is an indication of the pitching of tents for them and the lowering of curtains over them. A khaymah is the dwelling-place of a man, like a house made of wood, to the extent that the Arabs call a house of hair a khaymah because it is prepared for residence. Having established this, we say: His saying, ﴿secluded in pavilions﴾ is an indication of a meaning of the utmost subtlety, namely that the believer in Paradise has no need to move for anything; rather, things move towards him. Food and drink reach him without any movement on his part, and they are brought around to them whatever they desire. The houris dwell in tents, and when they move to the believers at the time of their desire, tents journey with them to set out towards the believers; and for the believers there are palaces, and the houris descend from the tents to the palaces. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾ has already had its interpretation given.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the arrangement (al-tartib), and in it there are several aspects:

The first: when Allah, the Exalted, concluded the blessings of this world with His saying, ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, He concluded the blessings of the Hereafter with His saying, ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, as an indication that what remains and endures in its own essence is Allah, the Exalted, alone, while the world is perishing; and the Hereafter, though it endures, its enduring is by the preservation of Allah, the Exalted.

The second: that in the closing verses of all these surahs He mentioned the name of Allah. In the surah before this one He said: ﴿In the seat of truth, with a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. And that the servant being in the presence of Allah is among the most complete blessings; likewise here, after mentioning the Gardens and the blessings in them, He said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, as an indication that the most complete blessing with Allah, the Exalted, and the most perfect pleasure, is the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. And in the surah after this one He said: ﴿Then rest and bounty and a Garden of delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89]. Then He said, Exalted is He, at the end of that surah: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96].

The third: that He, Exalted is He, mentioned all the pleasures in the Gardens but did not mention the pleasure of hearing, which is among the most complete kinds of it, so He said: ﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾, hearing the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.

The second issue: the root of tabaraka is from barakah, which means permanence and stability, and from it comes the kneeling of a camel (buruk al-ba'ir) and the pool of water (birkat al-ma'), since water remains in it constantly. In it there are several aspects:

The first: His name endures and is established.

The second: goodness endures with Him, for barakah, although it derives from stability, is used for goodness.

The third: tabaraka means exalted and elevated in status, not in place.

The third issue: after mentioning the blessings of this world He said: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], and after mentioning the blessings of the Hereafter He said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾, because the indication after enumerating the blessings of this world concerned the annihilation of every contingent thing and its passing away in its own essence; and the name of Allah, the Exalted, benefits those who remember Him, and there is no one there who declares the oneness of Allah to the utmost degree of tawhid, so He said: "And there remains the Face of Allah, the Exalted." The indication here concerns the fact that the enduring of the people of Paradise is by Allah's preserving them as those who remember the name of Allah, taking delight in it, so He said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾, i.e., on that Day no name remains except the name of Allah, the Exalted; the tongues revolve around it, no one has any need of another by mentioning him, and no one fears anyone; if they discuss, they discuss by the name of Allah.

The fourth issue: is the ism (name) superfluous (muqhaman), or is it a原 noun to which tabaraka is attributed? We say: there are two aspects:

The first, and this is the well-known view, is that it is superfluous, like the word "Face" in His saying, ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk: 1], and other usages of the word tabaraka.

The second: that the ism is tabaraka, and in this there is an indication of an eloquent meaning. If we say tabaraka means exalted, then how can the name of the one who is exalted be the one named? For when a king's status is great, his name is not mentioned except with a kind of veneration, and then when the one mentioning reaches him, his veneration of him is greater.

Page 121

For the utmost veneration of the name is that when the listener hears it he stands up, as is the custom of kings: when they hear in letters the name of a great sultan they stand at the hearing of his name; then if the sultan himself comes to them instead of his letter containing his name, they receive him and place their foreheads on the ground before him. This is among the clear proofs that the elevation of the name indicates an additional elevation in the one named. As for if we say: in the sense of "the good endures with Him", then it is an indication that the remembrance of the name of Allah, the Exalted, removes evil, drives away the devil, increases goodness and brings near felicities. And if we say: in the sense of "the name of Allah endures", then it is an indication of the enduring of those who remember Him in Paradise, according to what we said earlier.

The fifth issue: the well-known reading here is ﴿Possessor of Majesty﴾, and in His saying, ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty﴾, because majesty belongs to the Lord, and the name is other than the named. As for the face of the Lord, it is the Lord Himself; so there He described the Face, and here He described the Lord, not the name. If He had said "and the Lord remains", one might suppose that when the Lord remains Lord, He has a servant (marbub) at that time; but when He said "Face", the servant was set aside, and the certainty of enduring for the Truth was achieved; so the description "Face" conveys this benefit. And Allah knows best, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings be upon our master Muhammad, and his family, and his companions, and peace.
